news.title: An interview with John Ternus, who says the memory shortage is "a crisis" and "all options should be on the table", and that Tim Cook "has great relationships" (Andrew R. Chow/Time)
news.title_en: An interview with John Ternus, who says the memory shortage is "a crisis" and "all options should be on the table", and that Tim Cook "has great relationships" (Andrew R. Chow/Time)
news.author: Time
news.article_content:
Andrew R. Chow/Cupertino, Calif.Follow this author to personalize your feed and get instant alerts.

Devin Oktar Yalkin for TIMEJust below the broad smile he’s been wearing all morning, John Ternus’ hands are shaking.

On this September day in Silicon Valley, Apple’s new CEO is surrounded by celebrities, tech enthusiasts, and reporters who have flocked to Apple Park from around the world to catch a glimpse of the company’s new and long-awaited foldable phone, the Duo. After Ternus takes a few photos with the device, an Apple PR rep pulls the influencer known as IShowSpeed out of the crowd to meet him. Winning over the 21-year-old isn’t exactly the toughest assignment Ternus has faced in his 25-year Apple career: Speed barks when he sees the phone and then gleefully springs into a backflip.

Ternus, who took over as CEO on Sept. 1, was chosen to run Apple because he has ably applied his engineering and design expertise to shape products that redefined entire categories of technology, from the Mac to iPad to AirPods and the iPhone. But becoming the face and front man for the second biggest company in the world by market cap is another proposition entirely. Ternus’ hard technical skills may not translate easily to a position that involves toggling from Hollywood to stockholders, to politicians shaping policy, to rival CEOs in the constellation of tech companies whose power challenges nation-states.

His predecessor, Tim Cook, gained stature on the world stage as a power broker deftly navigating global politics, markets, and supply chains. Cook’s predecessor, Steve Jobs, was a rock-star visionary who sold the world on the deeply personal and even spiritual nature of tech creations. Ternus is different from both: a private, detail-oriented engineer, little known outside the company until he became a senior hardware executive in 2021.

Rather than try to replicate his forerunners’ styles of success, Ternus has so far played to his own strengths—which are also those of Apple, a company that first and foremost builds beautiful products that spark productivity, creativity, and joy. Ternus’ interaction with IShowSpeed is clearly designed to capture this (and, of course, to goose preorder numbers among the influencer’s young and massive audience). To some critics, however, the scene might read as a legacy company aura-farming to sell expensive gizmos instead of building the actual technological future, which is artificial intelligence.

Virtually every one of Apple’s fellow Goliaths—Microsoft, Google, Meta, Amazon, and now Nvidia, OpenAI, and Anthropic—have flung themselves into the AI arms race, pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into training ever more intelligent thinking machines. While Apple trains its own models, it is nowhere near the technology’s frontier, leaving the company vulnerable to being left behind if super-smart AI transforms industry and society in the coming years. At the end of September, Apple was conspicuously absent when President Donald Trump hosted a luncheon for AI power players like SpaceX’s Elon Musk, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, and Google’s Sundar Pichai, who lobbied him on their visions for America’s tech future.

But Ternus and other Apple executives say they aren’t concerned. In the midst of a populist AI backlash, they contend that they are building a modest but personalized and privacy-preserving form of AI that will actually help ordinary people as opposed to merely dazzling Silicon Valley’s “lunatic fringe,” as Greg Joswiak, senior vice president of worldwide marketing, puts it. And besides, Ternus argues, even if other companies succeed in their mission of building super-intelligence, users will still want to talk to it on Apple devices.

“People want physical things,” he says a week later at the company’s flagship store on Fifth Avenue in New York City, wearing an amiable but guarded smile. He spent the morning greeting superfans who had lined up all night to get their hands on the iPhone 18. “They want to talk, to see images of loved ones, to take pictures. So I don’t see a scenario where all of a sudden, our devices disappear and we don’t have a need for an iPhone.”

Ternus is barely older than the company he’s running. Born in 1975 in Orange County—Apple was founded in ’76, just 400 miles north—he grew up as Steve Jobs was redefining the personal computer as a societal force. When Ternus was 8 years old, his father bought an Apple II. “I started playing games on it and fell in love with Apple,” he says. A decade later, he took his family’s newer Mac, an SE model, to college at the University of Pennsylvania, where he studied mechanical engineering.

In 2001, Ternus left a virtual reality company to join Apple at 26 as an engineer. He has now spent half his life at the company, rising through the ranks on his propensity to consider both how products are made and how the user will experience them. “John was really at the center of driving the spirit of collaboration across the company to make sure that end-to-end these products give you that delightful experience—and the technology kind of disappears as you’re using it,” says Richard Dinh, Apple’s vice president of product design.

Over the past 15 years, some critics have accused Apple of failing to innovate the way it did in previous eras, when the company popularized the home computer, the MP3 player, and the smartphone. But it is undeniable that Apple’s core products—its computers and phones—have remained elite thanks to behind-the-scenes innovations in hardware and software. And Ternus, Apple executives say, has been a big part of these improvements.

When Cook, 65, announced in April he would step down following a 15-year tenure, it was no surprise that the company tapped Ternus as his successor. Other executives describe him as pragmatic, meticulous, and unifying. “Ternus is a logical pick,” says Neil Cybart, an analyst who has been following Apple for more than a decade on his site Above Avalon. “He has been a big believer in this design-first culture that defines Apple, as well as the idea that it’s not just technology here; there needs to be something more.”

In the late 2010s, Apple executives shifted their messaging to focus more on fast-growing services like iCloud, the App Store, and Apple Music. But growth in service revenue has moderated this year, and the promotion of Ternus, a hardware and product guru, signals a return to the company’s roots.

So it’s fitting that his ascension coincided with the announcement of the Duo, Apple’s most radical design change to the iPhone since its 2007 release. Apple has been exploring the concept for years. In 2011, when many people still carried around flip phones, Ternus and five other engineers filed a patent application for foldable electronic devices, exploring what kind of batteries and circuit boards might be needed for such an idea. “It felt clear that we were going to eventually get to a place where OLED displays were going to be flexible,” Ternus says.

Many challenges stood in between the patent and the final product. The first attempts at a foldable smartphone in the 2010s from other companies tended to be fragile and not all that useful, with a big, ugly crease in the center interrupting the experience. “The other examples in the world felt kind of cheap and crappy,” Ternus says.

Across hardware and software teams, Apple engineers and designers got to work. With advancements in Apple silicon chips, they created a new display engine that facilitates seamless transitions between the inner and outer screens. They redesigned iOS to move the phone’s main controls from the bottom to the right side for easier thumb access.

Along the way, Ternus encouraged the team to invest more time and effort in the project, even as other foldables beat them to market. Dinh says that at one point, he asked Ternus whether his team should proceed with a top surface material similar to those of its competitors, which Dinh felt had flaws but was potentially good enough.

“And he was like, ‘Look, Rich, you’ll know when it’s the right thing.’ And that gave us the confidence to really push the boundaries on innovation and manufacturing, and fly worldwide to connect our suppliers together and come up with the nanotexture [a surface technology],” Dinh says. The result—a surface made from a custom polymer and built atop a hinge with more than 100 tiny interior precision components—has impressed its first users, who have said they can barely detect a crease at all.

Ultimately, the Duo promises a passport-size phone that opens into a powerful tablet. Users can stow it in their pockets, then open it up and watch a movie on its matte, light-deflecting surface. They can compare websites side by side, play touchscreen games with intricate detail, and use a dual-camera setup to simultaneously show themselves and what they’re seeing on FaceTime.

Of course, the Duo’s success is far from guaranteed. It could go the way of Apple flops like the Apple Car, which was never released, or the Vision Pro, which had staggeringly low sales in the last year. Certainly many prospective buyers will blanch at the device’s $2,000-plus price tag.

The opening motion of the hinge on Apple's newest invention, the iPhone Duo. HAW-LIN SERVICES

A look inside the iPhone Duo's internal structure. HAW-LIN SERVICES

But the phone’s first public testers have given glowing feedback. And demand for the Duo’s closest rival, Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold8, has been strong, suggesting there is a growing appetite for the foldables category, especially in Asia.

Apple also hopes that the Duo will earn a cultural cachet among storytellers and other artists, many of whom, like loyal Apple customers, still regard the company more as a maker of useful tools rather than as the enemy Big Tech has become. Four-time Oscar winner Sean Baker (Anora), who spoke at a “no-AI” film festival earlier this year, attended the Duo announcement in Cupertino and described his relationship with Apple as collaborative. “It’s not just ‘buy or use our product’—it’s much more of a working relationship where they stay in touch and ask us for feedback,” he says.

Baker noted that Apple’s products often underpin many parts of the filmmaking process. For instance, when moviemakers need to add dialogue in postproduction, they often simply record on an iPhone, because it’s convenient and nearly production-grade.

In person, Ternus presents as a guy trying to blend in: he dresses in nondescript clothes and speaks in platitudes, often about the brilliance of Apple’s internal culture. He has devoted much of his early tenure as CEO to obsessing over design, spending multiple days a week in the studio with the industrial-design and human-interface teams.

But beyond Apple Park’s gleaming, curved walls, Ternus has tough choices to make. Case in point: the ongoing global shortage of memory chips, which has raised costs and delayed production timelines. In July, the Financial Times reported that Apple had begun testing memory chips made by a Chinese company as a way to increase supply. That drew a swift rebuke from a bipartisan group of Senators, who wrote a letter to Apple arguing that to do so would imperil national security.

Ternus pushes back on that idea. “The constraints in memory are absolutely a crisis,” he tells TIME in the second of two interviews during September. “So our fundamental belief is that all options should be on the table.”

Cook was skilled at managing relationships with governments around the world, vigorously defending Apple’s interests even if it made him a target of ridicule. His courtship of Trump, which included a widely maligned presentation of a disc with a 24-karat gold base at the White House in 2025, helped Apple secure relief from some of the Administration’s most punishing proposed levies.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 苹果核心硬件高管约翰·特纳斯（John Ternus）在独家访谈中坦言，全球内存组件短缺已经演变为硬件行业的全面危机，苹果正把所有可能应对的方案都摆上桌面。特纳斯同时强调蒂姆·库克拥有极其深厚的全球供应商人脉，公司正在硬件创新与上游核心零部件供应极度紧绷的夹缝中寻求平衡。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Apple hardware engineering leader John Ternus acknowledged that the global memory shortage has escalated into a full-blown crisis, stating all mitigation options are on the table. While navigating tight silicon supply, Ternus leaned on Tim Cook's formidable supply-chain connections to maintain operational stability.

news.content_snippet: Celebrate Teachers’ Day with AI for Educators in Brazilian Portuguese and see how Study Mode can help teachers support active, step-by-step learning.
news.summary_en: OpenAI introduced updates to its 'Study Mode' and educational offerings, focusing on active, inquiry-based learning. Instead of instantly generating answers, the model adopts a Socratic prompting framework to guide students step-by-step through critical thinking.

news.summary_zh: OpenAI为教育者升级学习模式，通过启发式多轮提问倒逼学生主动思考解题

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: OpenAI结合国际教师节活动，面向教育工作者升级了‘学习模式’（Study Mode）及多语言教育支持方案。该功能一改AI直接输出最终答案的作弊式交互，转为模仿苏格拉底式教学法，通过层层递进的提问引导学生逐步拆解问题并主动推导结论，旨在缓解教师对学生利用AI抄袭作业的深层担忧。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: OpenAI introduced updates to its 'Study Mode' and educational offerings, focusing on active, inquiry-based learning. Instead of instantly generating answers, the model adopts a Socratic prompting framework to guide students step-by-step through critical thinking.

elements_en.what: Enhanced Study Mode to encourage step-by-step reasoning rather than direct answers
elements_en.why: Address systemic concerns from teachers over AI cheating and reposition ChatGPT as an educational ally

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 以前学生用它一键秒出作业答案，现在它非要像教导主任一样反问你三道思考题。OpenAI这套‘苏格拉底人设’看似情操高尚，其实就是给全球愤怒的老师们灌一剂公关安慰剂——毕竟要是学校全禁了ChatGPT，下一代付费订阅用户可就断粮了。

news.title: BofA says it hired 1,000 contractors in Q2 to support 3,000 internal staff in patching proprietary and vendor software flaws exposed by AI models like Mythos (Hugh Son/CNBC)
news.title_en: BofA says it hired 1,000 contractors in Q2 to support 3,000 internal staff in patching proprietary and vendor software flaws exposed by AI models like Mythos (Hugh Son/CNBC)
news.author: CNBC
news.article_content:
Bank of America has hired an army of external contractors to help it patch software vulnerabilities exposed by advanced artificial intelligence models including Anthropic's Mythos, the bank's CEO, Brian Moynihan, told CNBC on Wednesday.

In an interview after the bank's third-quarter earnings release, Moynihan said that earlier this year the company rushed to bolster a wide spectrum of its internal and vendor code using thousands of employees and outside personnel.

"That risk is real risk, and that's why when the frontier-type models came out. … A lot of us sat down and said, 'How do we figure out how to get through this quickly?" Moynihan told CNBC's Leslie Picker.

"We put on 1,000 contractors to help us do the patching work in the second quarter, and those people remain here today, helping us, on top of the 3,000 people we have in that area," he said.

The bank spent a "couple hundred million plus" on the software remediation and regulatory issues related to anti-money laundering compliance in the third quarter, Moynihan told analysts earlier Wednesday.

The comments are some of the first by a major U.S. corporation to specify the manpower and dollars spent to protect software systems from Mythos, which was released to a small group of banks, technology firms and government agencies in April.

They also highlight the dual-edged nature of AI: While it can help companies save money by boosting productivity, the ability of models like Mythos to uncover and exploit decades-old software flaws has also forced firms into a costly defensive scramble.

"We've got to stay ahead of them, and we've got to be mindful that the people doing the software development are the people trying to sell us the services," Moynihan said.

Still, Moynihan — speaking as his company's shares slumped as much as 8% Wednesday — sought to reassure investors that the spending increase was temporary.

"Once you patch, you don't have to patch as much. … The pipeline moves through," Moynihan said, adding that the bank expects remediation costs to decline over time.

In other places, AI is helping to reduce expenses. Bank of America has about 130 internal AI projects, and savings from those efforts are expected to rise from $300 million this year to $700 million in 2027, Moynihan told analysts.

Bank of America's head count fell by about 3,400 employees in the past year as the firm cut roughly 5% of managers, he said. It's unclear how much of that workforce reduction is attributable to AI.

news.summary_zh: 美国银行雇佣上千名外部外包人员协助内部3000人团队，紧急修补前沿大模型暴露出的代码漏洞

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 在第三季度财报发布后的高管交流中，美国银行首席执行官布莱恩·莫伊尼汉披露，面对前沿人工智能大模型带来的安全审查冲击，公司在第二季度紧急雇佣了1000名外部技术外包人员。这批外包团队与美银内部3000名专职人员协作，紧急修复了涉及内部专有架构及第三方供应商的海量软件漏洞。该行本季度在软件漏洞整改及反洗钱合规等事项上已耗费数亿美元，成为首家公开量化AI安全应对成本的华尔街巨头。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Following the third-quarter earnings release, Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan revealed that the bank hired 1,000 external contractors in Q2 to help its 3,000 internal staff patch code vulnerabilities exposed by frontier AI models. The bank spent hundreds of millions of dollars on software remediation and AML-related compliance, marking one of the first explicit admissions by a major corporation of the massive costs required to secure systems against AI risks.

elements_en.where: Post-Q3 earnings interview and analyst conference
elements_en.what: Hired 1,000 contractors to assist 3,000 internal staff and spent hundreds of millions patching software flaws

ai_analysis.insight_zh: AI厂商天天在台上宣传大模型写代码提效十倍，金融巨头却在台下雇了几千个真人外包天天给AI擦屁股。所谓的科技降本增效，最终变成了大模型在前线疯狂制造或暴露漏洞，老牌银行在后方疯狂给外包公司打钱。
ai_analysis.insight_en: While AI vendors boast 10x coding productivity on stage, Wall Street giants are quietly hiring armies of human contractors to clean up the mess. The promised cost efficiency has morphed into AI finding bugs faster than humans can write checks to outsourced patchers.

Laying the foundation for the reinvention of the PC in the agentic AI era

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The hardware foundation for that vision of the future is now in place. Last week, we flew out to San Francisco to get all the details on the RTX Spark platform, and we returned home with Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra in top-end trim to put it all to the test.

This system has the full RTX Spark Superchip with 20 CPU cores and 6144 CUDA cores alongside 128GB of LPDDR5X-9400 RAM, and I’ve been putting it through its paces over the past week to see just what it can do.

The embargoes for the RTX Spark launch are a bit peculiar. Today, we’ll be sharing our broad experience with the Spark platform, as well as competitive performance evaluations, but not any system-specific results such as battery life, build or display quality, or other details of that nature. We have other RTX Spark laptops in the Tom’s Hardware labs, and detailed reviews of those systems will be coming soon.

No, this approach doesn’t make a lot of sense when the experience of a mobile platform is intimately and inextricably tied to the specific implementation of that chip in a particular laptop design. And we know that battery life is the first and foremost concern of many interested in this platform. But again, all that information is coming soon.

Microsoft and Nvidia launch Surface Laptop Ultra with RTX Spark 
                    
                
                            
                    
                            
    
    
    
                        Mystery reviewer 'finds' Nvidia RTX Spark prototype laptop and puts it through its paces
                    
                
                            
                    
                            
    
    
    
                        AMD attempts to get ahead of expected RTX Spark launch with Gorgon Halo benchmarks
                    
                
                    
    For this first round of testing, we compared the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra with RTX Spark against two systems. The first is a 14" MacBook Pro with Apple's highest-end M5 Max SoC inside. That Mac has a 40-core GPU and an 18-core CPU, as well as 128 GB of LPDDR5X RAM. We don't have a mobile Ryzen AI Max+ 395 system in the labs right now, but we do have AMD's compact Ryzen AI Halo as a source of fresh data with the latest ROCm stack and llama.cpp builds.

Judging local AI performance is a constantly moving target, and this review is no different. Our past testing has exercised the prompt processing and token generation phases of AI inference separately, with the understanding that a system that's fast at both those phases provides the best experience.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

But in an agentic workflow, that benchmarking technique doesn't capture the total time required to complete a task across all the inference turns needed to reach a particular goal. To capture that entire end-to-end time, the folks at Artificial Analysis have developed a new benchmark, AgentPerf-local, that precisely replays inference traces across several agentic AI tasks. The value of this approach should make immediate sense: the faster an AI agent finishes a job, the more productive a system can be.

So instead of presenting raw time-to-first-token and tokens-per-second figures, as we have in the past, we’re sharing time-to-completion values as we would for more traditional CPU and content creation benchmarks.

Again, local AI benchmarking is a continuous work in progress, so let us know what you think of this approach, and we’ll take that feedback into account as we continue to develop our methods.

Exploring Apple Silicon’s local AI performance with the Mac Studio and M4 Max
                    
                
                            
                    
                            
    
    
    
                        Chinese modder gets GeForce RTX 4060 working in Windows 11 on Huawei Arm workstation
                    
                
                            
                    
                            
    
    
    
                        Tom’s Hardware Innovation Awards 2026: Progress amid turmoil
                    
                
                    
    We ran AgentPerf-local with two compatible models: the dense Qwen 3.8-27B, which is popular as one of the most intelligent local models available for its size, and the Qwen 3.6 35B A3B mixture-of-experts model, which is less intelligent but easier for a wide range of systems to run quickly. We used the latest build of llama.cpp as our inference backend and built it from source on each test system to take advantage of CUDA, Metal, or ROCm acceleration, as appropriate.

Let’s look at Qwen 3.8 27B’s behavior first. We used Unsloth’s Q4_K_M quantization of the model. We ran it with DFlash2 speculative decoding on the RTX Spark and MacBook Pro, and with Qwen 3.8 27B’s built-in MTP on the Ryzen AI Halo for the best performance.

As we found in our benchmarking of Apple's Mac Studio with the M4 Max SoC, memory bandwidth is only one constraint for local AI performance. Despite its memory bandwidth advantage on paper, the M5 Max MacBook Pro still ends up taking about 25% longer to finish the AgentPerf benchmark with Qwen 3.8 27B than the Surface Laptop Ultra with RTX Spark.

Part of that may be down to software maturity, but it's also worth remembering that our Surface Laptop Ultra is a 15" system with a much larger 140W power adapter versus the 14" MacBook Pro's 96W charger.

news.title: Ledger unveils Atom, an $899 data-only Android-based smartphone companion device launching in summer 2027, as it pauses some sales following hardware tampering (Dominic Preston/The Verge)
news.title_en: Ledger unveils Atom, an $899 data-only Android-based smartphone companion device launching in summer 2027, as it pauses some sales following hardware tampering (Dominic Preston/The Verge)
news.author: The Verge
news.article_content:

Atom is a data-only Android device designed to work alongside your smartphone.

Atom is a data-only Android device designed to work alongside your smartphone.

Dominic PrestonCloseDominic PrestonNews EditorPosts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

ShareGiftThe Atom couldn’t have launched at a worse time for Ledger. Image: LedgerDominic PrestonCloseDominic PrestonPosts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Ledger has announced its latest crypto-centric hardware effort, the Android-based Atom, a device that resembles a phone but is instead designed to be used alongside one. It arrives at a tricky time for Ledger, which has been forced to cease sales of some of its hardware across southeast Asia following hardware tampering in its supply chain, which has reportedly seen over $86 million worth of crypto stolen from across some users’ accounts.

While Ledger’s previous hardware wallet signers have been compact devices, running custom software and often with E Ink displays, the Atom is the spitting image of a regular Android smartphone. In fact it essentially is an Android phone, except for the fact that its eSIM capabilities have been limited to data-only, with no support for texting or calls.

The Atom runs on both Android OS and Ledger OS, which sits on its own secure element chip, allowing you to move into a secure environment for tasks like crypto transactions. Two Atom users can also send encrypted messages to one another using regular Android messaging apps, with the messages decrypted within Ledger OS on the recipient’s device. Ledger has designed the device with AI agents in mind, including a partnership with OpenClaw, designed so that agents can handle financial tasks without getting full access to digital wallets, with physical approval required to complete transactions.

Next1/5Image: LedgerLedger says that the Atom is “not designed to replace your phone.” The company’s head of PR, Phillip Costigan, told me that Ledger recognized it was unlikely to be able to produce a device capable of competing with top Android handsets on camera and other specs, and so didn’t try to. The Atom is in fact intentionally limited in some respects: the 6.77-inch OLED display is only 60Hz, it runs on a Qualcomm Dragonwing chip rather than Snapdragon, and it only has a single rear camera and a 4,000mAh battery. Still, it will receive five years of Android OS updates, and at least seven years of support for spare parts, including a user-replaceable battery. It also has a physical privacy switch, which cuts power to the camera and microphone “at a circuit level.”

The launch couldn’t come at a worse time for Ledger. The company has confirmed reports that at least one of its hardware signers was sold by a reseller with “an unauthorized hardware implant,” which read users’ 24-word recovery phrases and transmitted them elsewhere using an eSIM. The discovery has forced Ledger to pause sales across southeast Asia, and at German retailer MediaMarkt. Reports suggest that over $86 million worth of crypto may have been stolen from across affected users, though Ledger hasn’t confirmed the scale of the losses.

That would be enough to give anyone pause before buying new Ledger hardware, at least from a third-party seller. Still, the company says that the Atom has been designed with physical anti-tampering measures, which it claims would have blocked the screen reader implants involved in the recent incident:

Core protection: A protective enclosure surrounds the Secure Element, MCU, and FPGA, and it is designed to detect any attempt to drill into or open this area.

Display and back cover detection: Ledger Atom detects when the display or back cover is removed. The back cover is paired with the device, so it cannot be swapped with a cover from another Ledger Atom.

Tamper-evident packaging: Ledger Atom’s packaging is designed to show whether it has been opened before it reaches you.

The Atom will be available from summer 2027. Reservations are open now, with a refundable $100 deposit to secure a Founder’s Edition device for $849. After the launch, the price will rise to $899.

Atom is a data-only Android device designed to work alongside your smartphone.

Atom is a data-only Android device designed to work alongside your smartphone.

Dominic PrestonCloseDominic PrestonNews EditorPosts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

ShareGiftThe Atom couldn’t have launched at a worse time for Ledger. Image: LedgerDominic PrestonCloseDominic PrestonPosts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Ledger has announced its latest crypto-centric hardware effort, the Android-based Atom, a device that resembles a phone but is instead designed to be used alongside one. It arrives at a tricky time for Ledger, which has been forced to cease sales of some of its hardware across southeast Asia following hardware tampering in its supply chain, which has reportedly seen over $86 million worth of crypto stolen from across some users’ accounts.

While Ledger’s previous hardware wallet signers have been compact devices, running custom software and often with E Ink displays, the Atom is the spitting image of a regular Android smartphone. In fact it essentially is an Android phone, except for the fact that its eSIM capabilities have been limited to data-only, with no support for texting or calls.

The Atom runs on both Android OS and Ledger OS, which sits on its own secure element chip, allowing you to move into a secure environment for tasks like crypto transactions. Two Atom users can also send encrypted messages to one another using regular Android messaging apps, with the messages decrypted within Ledger OS on the recipient’s device. Ledger has designed the device with AI agents in mind, including a partnership with OpenClaw, designed so that agents can handle financial tasks without getting full access to digital wallets, with physical approval required to complete transactions.

Next1/5Image: LedgerLedger says that the Atom is “not designed to replace your phone.” The company’s head of PR, Phillip Costigan, told me that Ledger recognized it was unlikely to be able to produce a device capable of competing with top Android handsets on camera and other specs, and so didn’t try to. The Atom is in fact intentionally limited in some respects: the 6.77-inch OLED display is only 60Hz, it runs on a Qualcomm Dragonwing chip rather than Snapdragon, and it only has a single rear camera and a 4,000mAh battery. Still, it will receive five years of Android OS updates, and at least seven years of support for spare parts, including a user-replaceable battery. It also has a physical privacy switch, which cuts power to the camera and microphone “at a circuit level.”

The launch couldn’t come at a worse time for Ledger. The company has confirmed reports that at least one of its hardware signers was sold by a reseller with “an unauthorized hardware implant,” which read users’ 24-word recovery phrases and transmitted them elsewhere using an eSIM. The discovery has forced Ledger to pause sales across southeast Asia, and at German retailer MediaMarkt. Reports suggest that over $86 million worth of crypto may have been stolen from across affected users, though Ledger hasn’t confirmed the scale of the losses.

That would be enough to give anyone pause before buying new Ledger hardware, at least from a third-party seller. Still, the company says that the Atom has been designed with physical anti-tampering measures, which it claims would have blocked the screen reader implants involved in the recent incident:

Core protection: A protective enclosure surrounds the Secure Element, MCU, and FPGA, and it is designed to detect any attempt to drill into or open this area.

Display and back cover detection: Ledger Atom detects when the display or back cover is removed. The back cover is paired with the device, so it cannot be swapped with a cover from another Ledger Atom.

Tamper-evident packaging: Ledger Atom’s packaging is designed to show whether it has been opened before it reaches you.

The Atom will be available from summer 2027. Reservations are open now, with a refundable $100 deposit to secure a Founder’s Edition device for $849. After the launch, the price will rise to $899.

news.title: The Download: reviving frozen pig kidneys and boosting nuclear power
news.title_en: The Download: reviving frozen pig kidneys and boosting nuclear power
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
Pig kidneys that were cooled to -150 °C and stored in a freezer for months have been successfully rewarmed and shown to work again for the first time, say scientists.

The kidneys, which are similar in size to human ones, were left in a glass-like state, in one case for over a year. Once they had been rewarmed, tested in machines, and transplanted into pigs, the kidneys regained their color and made urine—key signs they were working.

The results are a big milestone. But the team still needs to establish whether the approach could work for humans.

news.summary_en: In a major cryobiology breakthrough, scientists have successfully rewarmed pig kidneys stored at -150 °C for months—and in one instance for over a year—before transplanting them back into pigs where they regained color and produced urine. The vitrification method prevents ice crystal formation, offering a viable blueprint to overcome the fragile multi-hour preservation window of human donor organs.
news.title_zh: 零下一百五十度冷冻数月猪肾成功复温并完成移植
news.summary_zh: 科研团队成功复温玻璃化冷冻数月的哺乳动物肾脏并移植成活，实现排尿功能

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 在国际低温医学与器官移植领域，科研人员实现了一项里程碑式进展：在零下150摄氏度深低温冷冻长达数月乃至超过一年的猪肾脏，在被成功复温并移植至实验猪体内后恢复了血流与排尿功能。该实验采用玻璃化冷冻技术避免了冰晶对细胞组织的破坏，且复温后的器官大小与人类相当，为彻底突破传统供体器官仅数小时的极短保存窗口限制开辟了全新路径。

news.title: AI industry extinction warnings are genuine rather than corporate plots for regulatory capture or hype, and they go as far back as the mid-2000s and the 2010s (Scott Alexander/Astral Codex Ten)
news.title_en: AI industry extinction warnings are genuine rather than corporate plots for regulatory capture or hype, and they go as far back as the mid-2000s and the 2010s (Scott Alexander/Astral Codex Ten)
news.author: Astral Codex Ten
news.article_content:
In response, cynical commentators have suggested this is a conspiracy to boost the companies’ stocks. The exact motives imputed vary from person to person. Some say the companies are hyping the product by talking about how dangerous it is; if AI is smart enough to kill all humans, it must be smart enough for your business workflow. Others say they’re trying to distract from near-term harms; every inch of newspaper space devoted to human extinction is one less inch that can be spent on plagiarism and water use. But the most popular story involves regulatory capture: if the product is unsafe, maybe it can only be trusted to a few big politically-connected companies, and everyone else should be banned.

Many debates about AI are complicated and hard to resolve, but this one isn’t: all of these stories are clearly false. Some evidence:

The AI experts who aren’t affiliated with big companies are just as concerned as the ones who are.

The AI company leaders giving these warnings were giving the exact same warnings before they had AI companies - and in many cases, before they worked in the industry, or before the industry existed.

If these corporate plots were real, they would be incredibly dumb.

Grace et al surveyed 1,580 AI researchers who presented papers at big AI-related conferences, mostly academics with no company affiliation. Over half thought there was at least a 10% chance AI would cause “human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment of the human species”. 72% said we needed to be prioritizing AI safety research more. This survey was in 2024; current numbers would probably be higher.

Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, and Yann LeCunn are collectively considered “the godfathers of AI” for inventing deep learning; in 2018, they received the Turing Award, sometimes called the Nobel Prize of computer science, for their accomplishment. In 2023, Geoffrey Hinton quit his job at Google to work full-time raising awareness of the potential existential dangers of AI; he said there was “between 10% and 50% chance” that his invention would destroy humanity. In the same year, Yoshua Bengio also switched to activism, saying that he “regretted his life’s work” and that AI could have a “catastrophic impact”. Neither was affiliated with a major AI company.

Along with these independent researchers, there are many others who formerly worked at companies, then quit to whistleblow about the dangers, or left to pursue anti-AI activism full-time. Paul Christiano left OpenAI in 2021 to found an AI alignment nonprofit; he later said there was a “50/50 chance of doom shortly after you have AI systems that are human level.” Daniel Kokotajlo quit OpenAI in 2024, refusing to sign a non-disparagement clause even though it could have cost him $2 million in equity, in order to start a nonprofit warning about risks from AI (he says he thinks there’s about an 80% chance AI kills everyone). Jacob Coxon quit Anthropic in September, also likely giving up millions of dollars in equity, because he thought it was “gambling with our lives”. There are dozens of others.

The people at AI companies are no more likely to raise the alarm about AI dangers than people who were never at AI companies, or people who were previously at AI companies but have since quit.

He’s probably one of the people who’s I think done the most to promote clear thinking about the problem and tie it to current AI. We have a third person joining in a few weeks who I’m super excited about. We’re trying to build up a team that focuses on technical safety. We also do a little bit of strategy stuff which is how do we get different organizations that are working on AI to cooperate with each other, how do we cooperate with policy makers on questions like these. We’re also thinking a little bit about those issues but mainly technical safety.

Dario expanded on the cooperation point - he told the host about his fear that AI would lead to an “arms race” in which companies competed to develop the technology first and let safety slide. His solution was making companies cooperate:

We all think about AGI and think, that safety issues are important. . . then the question is, how does that scale to there being a lot of organizations? How does that scale to others who get involved once they see how powerful AI is? Can we make them cooperate as well? My hope is that we can.

This became an obsession with him, and he hired an advisor to help OpenAI work on the problem. According to the New Yorker:

In an early PowerPoint presentation to executives, Hedley outlined how OpenAI might avert a “catastrophic” arms race—perhaps by building a coalition of A.I. labs that would eventually coördinate with an international body akin to NATO, to insure that the technology was deployed safely.

As Hedley recalled it, [OpenAI president Greg] Brockman didn’t understand how this would help the company beat its competitors. “No matter what I said,” Hedley told us, “Greg kept going back to ‘So how do we raise more money? How do we win?’

This incident and several like it turned Dario against Greg, leading to an era of constant backstabbing office politics. Dario led a pro-safety faction against Greg’s pro-business faction; Greg usually won. It didn’t help that Dario was anxious to the point of paranoia, constantly insisting that their work was too dangerous to release:

Sam Altman tried to play peacemaker by promising Dario various concessions, but eventually Dario noticed that Altman lied constantly and never came through on any of them, so he and the rest of the safety faction left to found Anthropic. Here’s how Fortune described the split:

Amodei, along with a small group of employees, became concerned about OpenAI’s direction and what he perceived as a lack of safety involved in scaling up ChatGPT.

In 2021, Amodei, along with his sister and cofounder Daniela Amodei and a dozen other ex-OpenAI employees started Anthropic with a mission to put safety first. The company released its large language model, Claude, in 2023.

The employees who jumped ship from OpenAI believed two things, Amodei told Fortune’s Jeremy Kahn at the Fortune Brainstorm Tech conference in 2023. First, they believed if you pour more compute into large language models, they will greatly improve, and there’s almost no limit to how advanced they can get. Second, they believed—in addition to scaling up the models—there needed to be a strong set of guardrails and safety considerations.

SAM ALTMAN said in February 2015 - that is, ten months before he started OpenAI - that “development of superhuman machine intelligence is probably the greatest threat to the continued existence of humanity.” He continued:

The US government, and all other governments, should regulate the development of SMI [superhuman machine intelligence]. In an ideal world, regulation would slow down the bad guys and speed up the good guys—it seems like what happens with the first SMI to be developed will be very important.

Although my general belief is that technology is often over-regulated, I think some regulation is a good thing, and I’d hate to live in a world with no regulation at all. And I think it’s definitely a good thing when the survival of humanity is in question. (Incidentally, there is precedent for classification of privately-developed knowledge when it carries mass risk to human life. SILEX is perhaps the best-known example.)

He also famously said in June of that year that “AI will most likely lead to the end of the world, but in the meantime there will be great companies”. Some people say this was a “joke”. I think it was the one time in his life that Sam Altman was ever completely 100% honest.

His first statement on AI safety was in 2014, before he had any business ventures in AI, when he said that “We are summoning the demon with artificial intelligence”. He continued by calling it “our biggest existential threat”, and admitted that “I’m increasingly inclined to think there should be some regulatory oversight, maybe at the national and international level just to make sure that we don’t do something very foolish”.

Here’s a photo from the first big AI Safety conference in Puerto Rico. Elon is circled in orange. He was a rare famous billionaire who agreed to hang out with powerless nerds to debate the safety of a technology that technically didn’t exist yet, just for the love of the game.

The green circle is Demis Hassabis, the purple is Ilya Sutskever, and the red is Eliezer Yudkowsky.After the conference, Elon agreed to donate $10 million to the fledgling cause. He continued to be a regular at AI safety conferences over the next few years. I saw him speak at the Asilomar conference in 2017, where he gave a rambling talk on how brain-computer interfaces could solve the problem (they didn’t).

SHANE LEGG and DEMIS HASSABIS are two of the three co-founders of DeepMind, now Google DeepMind. In 2008 - a year before founding Deep Mind - Legg wrote his PhD thesis on “Machine Super Intelligence”, where he wrote that it could be “a nightmare scenario” (although he also said that “if we carefully prepare for this possibility in advance, not only might we avert disaster, we might bring about an age of prosperity unlike anything seen before.”) His other optimistic predictions include “If by suffering you mean prolonged suffering, then I think this is quite unlikely. If a super intelligent machine (or any kind of super intelligent agent) decided to get rid of us, I think it would do so pretty efficiently.”

news.title: Your secrets aren’t safe with this cute robot toy — they’re on Chinese servers ready to be hacked
news.title_en: Your secrets aren’t safe with this cute robot toy — they’re on Chinese servers ready to be hacked
news.author: The Verge AI
news.article_content:
There's a new digital pet in town - a cute little marshmallow of a robot that can change its cartoony expressions to match your mood. But if you or your kids talk to "Eiliko" over Wi-Fi, it'll phone home to China. Its AI companion can store literally everything you tell it on Chinese servers, where hackers can easily gain access or even hijack its personality. And the company that made it, Energize Lab, doesn't seem to care.

I bought an Eiliko from Amazon on August 29th. During a 10-minute conversation on August 30th, I asked the little bot: "Do you ever tell anybody else what I'm saying?"

"Your secrets are safe with me," it replied.

news.title: Citizen Lab details AdFection, a zero-click spyware campaign where an Israeli ad company routed targets to spyware servers and infected dozens of devices (Wired)
news.title_en: Citizen Lab details AdFection, a zero-click spyware campaign where an Israeli ad company routed targets to spyware servers and infected dozens of devices (Wired)
news.author: Wired
news.article_content:
Dubbing the attacks “AdFection,” the researchers documented a campaign in which an Israeli-registered advertising firm allegedly connected to the servers linked to a spyware company and infected dozens of devices with its invasive malware. Citizen Lab believes this to be the first detailed technical evidence made publicly available of sophisticated spyware infecting devices via digital ads.

Zero-click hacks are a holy grail for attackers and catastrophic for victims, because they can automatically install malware on devices without requiring any interaction or missteps from the target. When sophisticated hackers have deployed rare zero-click attacks in recent years, they have often exploited vulnerabilities in mobile messaging and communication apps to infect victims. But attackers have also exploited the sprawling infrastructure of the online ad ecosystem to distribute malware, sometimes with little or no interaction needed from victims. Evidence of the zero-click spyware campaign that Citizen Lab’s researchers uncovered shows the two threats merging, underscoring the extent and urgency of the risk.

“AdFection allows operators to automatically hack specific individuals with mercenary spyware as they use apps or browse the internet,” says Bill Marczak, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab. “Someone who gets hacked like this would not see anything amiss. In fact, they might not even see any ad at all.”

The situation is so concerning, he notes, because there isn’t much that people can do to protect themselves from zero-click ad attacks other than blocking ads as thoroughly as possible on all websites and platforms—a fact that intelligence agencies like the NSA and CIA seem to know all too well.

“The risk of having your device infected with spyware simply by using a website or app that displays ads is a nightmare scenario,” says Wolfie Christl, a senior Citizen Lab researcher.

During 2024 and 2025, Citizen Lab concluded that 45 devices belonging to the news outlet Al Jazeera were targeted with zero-click attacks delivered by ads. The researchers say that the targeted ads were issued by the Israeli-founded marketing firm Discover-Tech and distributed spyware attributed to the Israeli developer Candiru. Infected devices had contact with domains linked to Discover-Tech and then connected to infrastructure associated with Candiru, according to Citizen Lab’s analysis. (Al Jazeera, which participated in the investigation and shared device logs with Citizen Lab researchers, did not respond to a request for comment.)

“The ability to push individualized, arbitrary content at specific users is a hallmark of the modern online ads ecosystem, and is perfectly suited to the mercenary spyware industry,” Marczak says. “Until this architecture changes, or ad companies get serious about customer vetting, we’re going to keep seeing this kind of abuse.”

Emails and messages sent to Discover-Tech and its CEO by WIRED did not receive a response before publication. Integrity Partners, which is believed to own Candiru’s assets, following sanctions by the US government in 2021, also did not respond to requests for comment.

Google, which operates one of the world’s largest advertising businesses, terminated Discover-Tech’s registration after collaborating with Citizen Lab and researchers from the cybersecurity firm Confiant and confirming a spyware link. “Following a joint investigation with Citizen Lab and Confiant, Google blocked Discover-Tech from our ad platforms for systematically violating our policies,” a Google spokesperson says. “We also set up Safe Browsing warnings to help protect people if they navigate to websites linked to this group.”

The European branch of the  Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB), an ad industry body, confirmed to WIRED that it has suspended Discover-Tech from its global vendor list, known as the GVL. The company was suspended by IAB Europe following an audit of its policies, it says. “Further confirmation of the findings regarding spyware could also justify a definitive expulsion from the GVL,” a spokesperson for IAB Europe says.

A spokesperson for Beeswax, an online advertising industry company owned by Comcast, says in a statement: “Beeswax removed Discovery-Tech from our platform following recent activity and independent validation by a third-party security specialist. We maintain a zero-tolerance policy for malicious advertising.”

Often when you see ads online or in apps, they’re displayed following a complex process known as real-time bidding—essentially an automated auction where advertisers place bids to show you specific ads. The milliseconds-long process can result in advertisers collecting huge volumes of data about your device, your location, and browsing history, plus a whole lot more. The process has been a privacy nightmare for years, with murky data brokers selling people’s personal information, and law enforcement agencies and hostile nations buying it to track or target people.

The Citizen Lab researchers say that Discover-Tech operates an advertising platform, Controlium, that can allow its users to “de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices” once an ad appears. Overall, the researchers estimate that millions of devices were directed to Candiru’s servers, where they could be profiled. By analyzing ad-bidding records that were publicly exposed on the Discover-Tech website, the Citizen Lab researchers say, ads linked to the firm with attacker script tags were shown in more than 70,000 mobile apps and more than 120,000 websites between March and June this year. Multiple apps, the researchers say, displayed more than a million ads linked to Discover-Tech.

The firm’s ads weren’t necessarily all weaponized to potentially distribute spyware, but the researchers say that, in general, they have seen Discover-Tech ad impressions on government and national-security-linked networks around the world. These include NATO and United Nations networks, as well as lawmaking bodies in Europe, critical infrastructure providers in Australia, plus armed forces and government agencies in Norway and Sweden.

Previous zero-click targeted ad campaigns that distribute spyware have rarely surfaced publicly, but the Citizen Lab researchers say this is likely a symptom of ad infrastructure being so extensively trusted and incorporated in all aspects of digital life without specific oversight.

“The network logs from Al Jazeera were key in understanding the ad-based nature of that attack,” Marczak says. “If a user’s personal device were targeted, say, while they were connected to their home Wi-Fi or mobile data, there’s not going to be the same level of network monitoring there. So I think the lack of prior reporting is probably mainly a visibility issue: Defenders have to be in the right place at the right time, looking at the right data.”

Speaking generally about threats that can result from the sheer ubiquity of the digital ad ecosystem, Jason Kint, CEO of the digital media trade organization Digital Content Next (WIRED parent company Condé Nast is a member), says these kinds of attacks are both plausible and damaging.

“Although rare and sophisticated, I wouldn’t be entirely surprised to learn about zero-click attacks through ads,” Kint says. “Anything that goes directly against users’ expectations or lowers the trust in the open web is deeply concerning.”

(Pew Research Center illustration)




Pew Knight Initiative

The Pew-Knight Initiative supports new research on how Americans absorb civic information, form beliefs and identities, and engage in their communities.

Pew Research Center is a nonpartisan, nonadvocacy fact tank that informs the public about the issues, attitudes and trends shaping the world. Knight Foundation is a social investor committed to supporting informed and engaged communities. Learn more >

This report from the Pew-Knight Initiative focuses on online community and connection today. It looks at who’s part of online communities, where they form, what they’re built around, why people go to them – and why some people leave. It also examines what people think the internet is doing to connection overall.

The Center conducts research to inform the public, journalists and decision-makers. We’ve long studied what online connection looks like for Americans. At a time when fewer than half of Americans are highly satisfied with their social life – or with the quality of life in their local community – it’s important to understand the role online communities play, good and bad.

We surveyed 9,750 U.S. adults from May 26 to June 1, 2026. Everyone who took part in this survey is a member of the Center’s American Trends Panel. The survey represents the views of the full U.S. adult population.

Here are the survey questions used for this report, the detailed responses and the methodology.

This is a Pew Research Center report from the Pew-Knight Initiative, a research program funded jointly by The Pew Charitable Trusts and the John S. and James L. Knight Foundation. Find related reports online at https://www.pewresearch.org/pew-knight/.

At a time when many are worrying about fraying social ties and rising loneliness, some Americans are finding community online.

A new Pew Research Center survey from the Pew-Knight Initiative finds that nearly four-in-ten U.S. adults are part of an online community – and that share rises to about half among young adults.

For some, these communities are deeply valuable parts of their lives. They widely offer information, advice or experiences people say they could only get online.

Still, these benefits sit alongside doubts about making genuine connections online. About half of Americans question whether online relationships can be as meaningful as those formed in person. Fewer – 34% – think they can be just as meaningful.

There’s an age divide on this topic as well. Adults under 30 are far more likely than those ages 65 and older to say online relationships can be just as meaningful as in-person ones (54% vs. 14%).

Our questions asked about feeling part of a community online. We wanted to capture a wide range of spaces and experiences that someone might consider as online community. Here’s how we explained the topic further:

By this, we mean people connecting with others online, such as by joining or feeling part of a group or doing things together. This could happen in places like social media, online discussion forums, by emailing or messaging with a group, or in video games online.

Follow-up questions focused on the community people spend the most time in – we call this their most-visited online community.

More than two decades after the Center studied online communities in 2001, these spaces still vary in where they form, what they offer and who turns to them.

It’s most common to find online community on social media. About a quarter of Americans are part of an online community on social media sites or apps.

Discussion forums come next – 15% are part of an online community in places like Reddit, Nextdoor or Discord.

Fewer are part of an online community on video sites like YouTube and Twitch, in video games online, or on messaging apps.

And 5% are part of one on sites or apps for people who share a hobby – like Goodreads for reading, Strava for running, Ravelry for knitting or Letterboxd for movies.

When it comes to what these communities focus on: Hobbies and local area top the list. About one-in-five Americans say they are part of an online community related to each.

Roughly one-in-ten adults say they’re in one about topics like movies, books or TV shows; video games; or their work or profession. A similar share says they’re in fan communities of any kind.

And while politics can come up in a range of places, 8% of Americans are in an online community specifically related to politics or political issues.

Age, again, is an important factor: Young adults are more likely than all other groups to be part of several kinds of communities. For example, that’s true for online communities about video games; beauty or fashion; movies, books or TV shows; hobbies; and fan communities.

Gaming has one of the biggest gaps. About a quarter of adults under 30 (27%) are part of one about video games. This drops to 16% of those in their 30s and 40s and 4% of those 50 and older.

Participation also varies by other factors. Some examples are:

For more on who’s part of an online community in general, go to the appendix.

Online communities are widely seen as unique spaces and can add deeply to people’s lives.

About a quarter of those in online communities say these places are highly valuable to them. A larger share – about four-in-ten – finds some value there.

news.title: How much more can nuclear power plants give?
news.title_en: How much more can nuclear power plants give?
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
In this age of rising electricity demand, people are trying to squeeze every last bit of power out of every power plant possible.

Over the past few weeks, there’s been big news about nuclear power plants trying to do just that. Constellation, the largest nuclear operator in the US, announced plans to add nearly a gigawatt of new capacity across 11 existing nuclear reactors at six plants. And on October 5, the Department of Energy awarded a $4.2 billion loan to Vistra for previously announced upgrades at three plants.

Pushing existing reactors to produce more could help provide more clean power for data centers, quickly. But just how much additional power can we count on?

news.title: Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind
news.title_en: Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
Have you ever thought about what makes you you? Science assures us it has everything to do with the three-pound organ between our ears, with its billions of neurons and trillions of delicate connections. But it’s a lot trickier to explain why we have a sense of self-awareness or to pin down precisely where that first memory of Mommy actually resides. As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you.

To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are working on ways to keep your brain going—even beyond death. Let’s call them the “mind savers.” They’re exploring everything from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones to uploading our memories to the cloud. Here, we look at six possible paths for keeping your mind going, how feasible they’d be, and what benefits the ­present-day research might bring—even if cognitive immortality doesn’t pan out.

news.title: Pig kidneys that were “frozen” for a year have been brought back to life
news.title_en: Pig kidneys that were “frozen” for a year have been brought back to life
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
Pig kidneys that were cooled to -150 °C and stored in a freezer for months have been successfully rewarmed and shown to work again for the first time, say scientists. They hope to replicate the findings with human organs.

The kidneys—which are similar in size to human ones—were left in a glass-like state, in one case for over a year. Once they had been rewarmed, tested in machines, and transplanted into pigs, the kidneys regained their color and made urine—key signs they were working.

“Ten years ago … I wouldn’t say I had high hopes it was actually going to work,” says Erik Finger, a transplant surgeon at the University of Minnesota who co-led the work. “After we did the last transplant, I walked out of the room and said, ‘This is a big deal.’” The research was shared at the preprint server bioRxiv and has not yet been peer-reviewed.

news.author: TechCrunch
news.article_content:

Figma announces new features to define how agents work on its platform																				
				
																									
						

	
									
									
										

			Ivan Mehta
	

									
									
								
					
					
						9:30 PM PDT · October 14, 2026											
																			
					
		
	





			
					
		
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
	





	
	
		
		
			
Design platform Figma announced a new Markdown-based editor to help define a company’s design, bring in design and code libraries, and integrate with the Payload headless content management system during the company’s first Config event in India. Through some of these features, the company aims to provide a definition for its own and third-party agents to adhere to a brand’s design rules better while creating with AI.

The company debuted a new feature called Figma Specs, which is a markdown editor that lets users define their design language in a simple way. The document can serve as a reference for teams and agents while designing in Figma. Specs can exist as a standalone file in Figma or can co-exist within the canvas. Apart from acting as a text editor, users can reference other Figma elements, such as elements on the canvas and embed FigJam diagrams, code layers, and designs.

What’s more, teams can bring in more context about design, including design libraries, code libraries, and guidelines to manage context for the design system. Agents can also refer to this centralized system to adhere to rules.

In the past week, the company made its agent on canvas available to a wider user base. However, given the non-deterministic nature of AI, the company is providing tools to steer it towards more predictable outcomes.

“We see Figma as the place where software teams come to decide what they build and ship. And so for that, I think one of the key things to keep in mind about what AI has changed and what it made available is the ability to build,” Figma’s chief design officer Loredana Crisan told TechCrunch. “There are 17-times more lines of code being produced today than in the past. But when you’re looking at releases, only 1.3-times more releases. A lot of that code actually is not necessarily built to ship, but really built to discover what the product is. It’s built to design.”

The company said it is also supporting over 20 new tools with its MCP, including Open Code, Dia, Grok Bot, and Indian AI startup Sarvam.

Last year, Figma acquired open-source headless CMS Payload. Now, the company is integrating it with its Figma Make product for generating dynamic websites and directly managing content. The company said that Payload’s downloads have increased sixfold in the last 12 months.

The company opened its first office in India late last year with sales, partnership, go-to-market, and product support functions. Figma said that the country is its biggest market in terms of users outside the United States. The company noted that the platform works with 40% of India’s top 100 companies listed on the Bombay Stock Exchange.

news.title: TSMC reports Q3 revenue up 50.9% YoY to $46.36B, net income up 68.7% to $23.7B, both above est., marking a sixth straight quarterly profit record on AI demand (Jenny Lee/CNBC)
news.title_en: TSMC reports Q3 revenue up 50.9% YoY to $46.36B, net income up 68.7% to $23.7B, both above est., marking a sixth straight quarterly profit record on AI demand (Jenny Lee/CNBC)
news.author: CNBC
news.article_content:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. on Thursday reported a record third-quarter profit that beat estimates, powered by an unrelenting global appetite for AI chips.

Here are TSMC's third-quarter results against LSEG SmartEstimates, which are weighted toward forecasts from analysts who are more consistently accurate:

The world's largest contract chipmaker posted a record net profit for a sixth straight quarter, reporting 68.7% surge in the reported quarter from a year earlier.

TSMC's third-quarter operating margin came in at 58.7%, exceeding the upper end of its guidance range of 58%, showcasing the pricing power enjoyed by the company as the AI boom fuels demand for semiconductors.

TSMC forecast fourth-quarter revenue between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion, representing a 14% sequential increase and a 58% jump from a year earlier at the midpoint of its guidance range, according to the company's earnings call.

The chipmaker expects its capital expenditure from 2026 to 2028 to be significantly higher than in the previous three years, as it continues to ramp up investments to support growing customer demand.

TSMC's stronger-than-expected results and upgraded full-year revenue outlook underscore how demand for advanced chips continues to outpace its production capacity, with the company's elevated capital spending reflecting confidence in sustained growth over the coming years, Sravan Kundojjala, an analyst at SemiAnalysis, told CNBC via email.

TSMC expects its fourth-quarter business to be supported by continued strong demand for its advanced chipmaking technologies, including the ramp-up of its 2-nanometer process.

Kundojjala also highlighted TSMC's careful approach to capacity expansion, adding that the chipmaker is assessing whether customers have the financing and supporting components needed to deploy AI systems.

"Even after those checks, TSMC says demand remains well above its supply capacity," he said, adding that it reinforces confidence in the AI buildout while ensuring investment decisions reflect customers' ability to deploy the chips they order.

Advanced technologies, defined as 7-nanometer and more advanced technologies, made up for 79% of TSMC's total wafer revenue in the reported. The 3-nanometer chips accounted for the largest share of its revenue in the third quarter at 33%, followed by 5- and 7-nanometer chips.

By platform, high-performance computing accounted for the largest share of revenue at 68%, followed by smartphones at 21%. Meanwhile, automotive was the fastest-growing segment on a quarter-on-quarter basis, with 23%  growth rate.

TSMC said demand for AI chips remains strong, driven by the growing adoption of agentic AI and open-source AI models, which are expected to make AI more accessible and fuel demand for advanced semiconductors.

The company's free cash flow surged to NT$476.56 billion in the third quarter, from NT$139.38 billion a year ago.

TSMC also pointed to rising demand for AI accelerators, processors used in agentic AI applications and networking, adding that semiconductors are set to play an increasingly important role in the global AI supply chain.

TSMC also said it had completed construction of its second fab in Arizona and is installing equipment, with mass production expected to begin in the third quarter of 2027, slightly ahead of its previous schedule.

TSMC board approved NT$7.00 cash dividend for the second quarter. During its second-quarter earnings announcement in July, TSMC had outlined plans to expand its U.S. manufacturing footprint, including a total planned investment of $265 billion in Arizona.

The chipmaker is also reportedly considering expanding beyond Arizona, evaluating a potential investment in Texas as it looks to further strengthen its U.S. manufacturing presence.

news.title: Global smartphone shipments fell 22% YoY to 255.3M in Q3, a record quarterly drop, as Samsung and Apple gained while Xiaomi, Oppo, and Vivo saw deeper declines (IDC)
news.title_en: Global smartphone shipments fell 22% YoY to 255.3M in Q3, a record quarterly drop, as Samsung and Apple gained while Xiaomi, Oppo, and Vivo saw deeper declines (IDC)
news.author: IDC
news.article_content:
BOSTON, October 14, 2026 – The global smartphone market shrank 22.0% year-on-year to 255.3 million units in the third quarter of 2026 (3Q26), according to the preliminary data from IDC Research (IDC) Worldwide Quarterly Mobile Phone Tracker, Shipments tanked 22% year-on-year (YoY) in 3Q26, marking the highest YoY decline to date of any quarter as the AI-led memory crisis continue to disrupt the smartphone market with rapidly escalating component costs to unprecedented levels and strained supply.

“The sharp downturn the industry has been bracing for finally materialized in the third quarter this year, with shipments declining a record 22% YoY. However, the worst is yet to come,” said Nabila Popal, senior research director for Worldwide Devices, IDC. “Current indicators suggest that the market has not yet reached the bottom. Memory costs have surged approximately 350% since last year and are still rising, creating substantial pressure on vendor margins and shipments. While memory inflation is beginning to slow down, with a low double-digit sequential increase in Q3 compared to roughly 50%-100% sequential growth in prior quarters, costs remain elevated across other critical components as well, compounding the crunch.”

IDC expects market growth to be constrained through 2027 with any possible recovery pushed to 2028 at the least. Most importantly, OEMs are increasingly recognizing that they are facing a permanent structural shift in industry cost dynamics. While the outlook is challenging, periods of disruption also create opportunities for winners to emerge, making strategic execution and innovation more critical than ever. Vendors that adapt their product, pricing, and demand generation strategies to a higher cost structure will be best positioned to gain share.

“The third quarter shows the full impact and damage of the memory crisis,” said Francisco Jeronimo, vice president for Worldwide Devices, IDC. “The pressure is now moving from vendors to consumers. As higher prices reach the shelf, many buyers are keeping their current devices longer. Chinese brands face a particularly difficult moment, as their exposure to low-end smartphones forces them to choose between protecting margins and defending volume just as demand weakens. Volumes will stay under pressure in the coming quarters, while vendors with scale, secure supply and a premium mix keep gaining share in a smaller market.”

“While vendor ranking remains similar to last quarter, Samsung and Apple continue to gain share as players like Xiaomi, OPPO, vivo shipment declines intensify. As prices rise, consumers who can’t put off a purchase are likely best served by holiday-quarter offers, when promotions and discounts are expected to be at their most attractive, than wait for prices to ease. ” said Kiranjeet Kaur, associate research director for Worldwide Devices, IDC. “Despite the sluggish sales, some vendors raised production plans ahead of an expected tightening in component supply next year. If demand remains weak, this could lead to inventory build-up heading into 2027, adding a further downside risk to our 2027 forecast.”

Using proprietary tools and research processes, IDC’s Trackers are updated on a semiannual, quarterly, and monthly basis. For more information visit https://www.idc.com/data-analytics/.

news.title: Bloomberg is making its ASKB conversational AI interface available to all Terminal users, letting them integrate their own content with existing financial data (Steven Rosenbush/Wall Street Journal)
news.title_en: Bloomberg is making its ASKB conversational AI interface available to all Terminal users, letting them integrate their own content with existing financial data (Steven Rosenbush/Wall Street Journal)
news.author: Wall Street Journal
news.original_content:
Steven Rosenbush / Wall Street Journal:
Bloomberg is making its ASKB conversational AI interface available to all Terminal users, letting them integrate their own content with existing financial data  —  Allowing users to add their own information to the company's
news.content_snippet: Allowing users to add their own information to the company's generative AI-based ASKB interface will feed the system with a new level of context
news.summary_en: Bloomberg is rolling out its conversational AI interface, ASKB, to all Bloomberg Terminal subscribers. The system enables financial professionals to seamlessly merge proprietary internal data with Bloomberg's market data and analytical tools. This move aims to counter emerging enterprise AI competitors by satisfying Wall Street's demand for integrated generative financial intelligence.
news.title_zh: 彭博社正在向所有终端用户提供其 ASKB 对话式人工智能界面，让他们将自己的内容与现有的财务数据集成
news.summary_zh: 彭博面向所有终端用户开放对话式AI工具ASKB，支持用户将私有数据与专业金融库深度融合检索

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 彭博正式向所有彭博终端订阅用户全面开放其研发的对话式人工智能界面ASKB。该功能打破了以往仅依赖标准金融数据库的限制，允许金融机构和交易员将自身的专有研究报告、客户私有数据无缝嵌入彭博既有的海量行情与分析库中进行混合问答。此举旨在应对华尔街日益旺盛的内部大模型定制需求，防止高净值客户被第三方生成式AI金融工具分流。

news.content_snippet: Dutch semiconductor equipment giant ASML expects China to account for about 20 per cent of its total sales this year …
news.summary_en: Semiconductor lithography giant ASML projects that mainland China will account for approximately 20% of its total net sales this year. Driven by massive capacity additions in mature nodes, ASML's sales in China surged 109% quarter-on-quarter in Q3, lifting the region's share of total machine sales from 14% to 23%. This sustained influx reflects domestic fabricators actively securing non-restricted mainstream tools ahead of anticipated export restrictions.

news.title: Asian chipmakers extend Wall Street losses as US Fed rate hike fears and AI funding worries mount; SK Hynix fell 10%+ on the KRX, while Samsung fell ~10% (Lee Ying Shan/CNBC)
news.title_en: Asian chipmakers extend Wall Street losses as US Fed rate hike fears and AI funding worries mount; SK Hynix fell 10%+ on the KRX, while Samsung fell ~10% (Lee Ying Shan/CNBC)
news.author: CNBC
news.article_content:
A sell-off in global technology hardware stocks deepened Thursday, with Asian chipmakers tracking Wall Street losses as concerns over further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes, financing of artificial intelligence investments weigh on sentiment.

South Korean chip giant SK Hynix plunged over 10%, while rival Samsung Electronics fell 7.1%. Other South Korean chip-related stocks also came under pressure. LG Innotek sank 8.1%, Seoul Semiconductor shed 7.7% and Samsung SDI declined 6.8%.

In Japan, technology investment giant SoftBank Group tumbled 7.9%. Semiconductor testing equipment maker Advantest dropped 6.9%, while chipmaking equipment supplier Tokyo Electron lost 5.4%. Renesas Electronics declined 5.4%.

The declines come as investors grow increasingly concerned that higher borrowing costs could weigh on the massive capital spending required to build out AI infrastructure, putting pressure on technology companies that have benefited from the AI investment boom.

Chief executives of Broadcom and Intel warned on Monday that financing could become a major headwind to the AI boom, with Broadcom's Hock Tan saying it could be bigger challenge to AI expansion than shortages of chips or electricity.

The sell-off followed a bruising session on Wall Street Wednesday, where technology shares led broader market losses after hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data fueled concerns that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates further.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.88% to close at 26,692.87, while the S&P 500 shed 1.11% to end at 7,718.94. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.09%.

Dan Ives, tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the latest sell-off in AI-related stocks reflects growing concerns over the cost of financing massive infrastructure projects as U.S. Treasury yields climb above 5%, but added that underlying demand for AI computing power remains robust.

"Higher yields raise the cost of financing these builds, and investors are right to focus on balance sheets and contract structure, but rates are a financing question, not a demand question," Ives said in a note.

The latest pullback presents a buying opportunity, Ives said, adding that the AI infrastructure boom remained in its early stages despite mounting concerns over funding costs.

"What would change our view is a demand signal, not a rate signal," he said, pointing to potential cuts in hyperscaler capital expenditure plans, canceled contracts or falling GPU rental prices as warning signs.

news.summary_en: ByteDance is in advanced discussions to procure datacenter Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs) from chipmaker MediaTek.
