In May 2025, a 25-year-old man detonated a car bomb outside a Palm Springs fertility clinic, killing himself and injuring four others. For many, it was a wake up call about the threats to reproductive care facilities. For the FBI, though, it was also a sign of what the agency had feared for years: bad actors were using generative AI to plan and execute terror plots.

The suspect used an unnamed generative AI tool that failed to detect his request for bomb-making instructions, law enforcement officers wrote in a previously unreported document reviewed by the Guardian. The privacy of his conversation with the AI chatbot hindered alerting police that someone was looking up how to make a bomb, according to the memo.

FBI officers fear the scenario is set to repeat itself: “Threat actors will likely increase their use of GenAI tools for attack planning,” said the memo, which was distributed by the bureau’s Los Angeles division in May 2026. “Current built-in GenAI safeguards are insufficient to prevent illicit use as malicious actors successfully employ ‘jailbreaking’ techniques to access dangerous information.”

AI executives and staff at leading AI companies have focused their public remarks on potential doomsday scenarios, a long-term, hypothetical harm of the technology they’re developing. Law enforcement officers, by contrast, have been grappling with what they fear are the present-day threats that AI enables, including violent crimes.

A previously unreported cache of law enforcement and intelligence agency documents show that law enforcement agencies have, since 2021, considered AI both a tool and a target of would-be terrorists. Law enforcement has been trying to keep pace with the ways bad actors may be using AI for harm, concerned that the rapidly evolving technology may supercharge new and existing types of crimes.

At the same time, as public sentiment over AI and its impacts on society and the environment has soured, agencies have sought to protect AI infrastructure. The documents show police and intelligence officers are closely monitoring online opposition to datacenters among various groups with what they describe as extremist ideologies.

How extremists could use AI to devise attacks and recruit new members

How AI could be used to disseminate and produce everything from deepfakes to election misinformation and child sexual abuse material (CSAM)

How people seeking information on how to make weaponry or bombs could use AI to circumvent police detection

How to ensure that officers could take advantage of AI tools in policing, for things like social media monitoring, while managing public concern over the use of these tools

Monitoring social media for opposition to AI and potential extremist attacks on datacenters

The FBI did not respond to detailed questions on its monitoring of anti-AI sentiment and use of AI, but pointed to a general fact sheet on the agency’s use of the technology.

The NYPD stated that its threat analysis report on artificial intelligence was related to the “AI 2027” project – an influential forecast from several AI researchers that speculated about the technology’s rapid growth and the threats it could present. In one of the project’s possible futures, it predicted bioweapon-armed drones wiping out humanity.

“This NYPD Intelligence Analysis Report contained a summary and assessment of AI 2027,” the NYPD said. “It was distributed to appropriate NYPD members and partners for their awareness, as part of the Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau’s mission of analyzing developments and trends that have implications for public safety and national security.”

DHS said it “prioritizes the safety and security of Americans and remains committed to mitigating all forms of ideologically-motivated violence”, and regularly shares intelligence with state and local law enforcement related to threats from violent extremists.

“DHS threat assessments draw on available intelligence, law-enforcement information, and other reporting to inform partners of evolving threats,” DHS said in a statement. “DHS assesses that malicious actors may seek to use artificial intelligence to enhance existing harmful activities, including cyber-enabled activity, fraud schemes, and the production or dissemination of violent extremist propaganda”.

Law enforcement’s concerns over AI and extremism fall into two broad categories, the documents show. One focuses on the burgeoning threat of extremists using new tools such as generative AI to plot attacks or promote their ideology. The other involves extremists targeting the modern technology that underpins society and has a long history within far-right movements.

Before mainstream, widespread opposition to datacenters swept the US, there was a strain of violent extremism that targeted tech facilities and other critical infrastructure, hoping such terrorism could lead to the collapse of society and instigate a race war.

Law enforcement officers expressed concern over the threat these militias posed to datacenters’ security before the 2022 launch of ChatGPT. Several bulletins, such as an October 2021 joint threat analysis from DHS, National Counterterrorism Center and FBI, highlighted a plot by Seth Pendley, a January 6 rioter and far-right militia member, to blow up an Amazon Web Services facility.

“Pendley believed a successful attack on the Amazon facility would disrupt 70 percent of Internet service, expose perceived abuses of power, and lead to revolution,” the bulletin said. Pendley pleaded guilty to a charge of malicious attempt to destroy a building with an explosive and was sentenced in 2021 to 10 years in prison for plotting the attack.

Although law enforcement has long tracked extremist militia threats to infrastructure like Pendley’s, the documents show that in the years since the generative AI boom began, agencies more frequently expressed concern over anti-tech and anti-datacenter sentiment. Multiple fusion centers – law enforcement hubs for collecting information and coordinating between agencies – around the US warned of growing threats from domestic violent extremists – pointing to posts across social media platforms, messaging apps and forums like 4chan in which commenters vowed to destroy datacenters.

“I bring a sort of ‘tannerite and gasoline’ vibe to ai data centers,” an account associated with a white supremacist posted on Facebook last year, according to a 2025 Philadelphia police department intelligence bulletin. Combining gasoline with Tannerite, a brand of well-known explosive compound, produces a large and fiery detonation.

On some far-right forums, users discussed killing CEOs of AI companies and local officials who support datacenters, agents warned, as well as arson and bombing attacks against data facilities.

Law enforcement also monitored real-world anti-datacenter incidents or protests, including a demonstration in Michigan in March where the documents said that three people allegedly associated with a white supremacist group held a banner opposing what they called a “Jewish data center” being built in the state.

As opposition to artificial intelligence and datacenters have become more widespread, however, questions have risen over how law enforcement agencies’ tracking anti-datacenter and anti-tech ideology may bleed over into surveillance of nonviolent protest movements. Distrust of the AI industry and mobilization against datacenters has now become so prevalent that it is a mainstream issue of the midterm elections, far from an extremist position.

The documents show agencies casting a wide net as they track opposition to the tech industry, including broadly monitoring public social media and opposition such as proposed legislation against datacenters. In a Nevada Threat Analysis Center report from April 2026, law enforcement cited a local city council hearing on a datacenter moratorium as part of a trend of increased negative sentiment towards the facilities.

Some experts and activists have expressed concern that as mobilization against datacenters grows, peaceful anti-AI organizations could face surveillance from authorities.

“There’s nothing extreme about not wanting to lose your livelihood to AI, your drinking water to AI datacenters, your privacy to ubiquitous AI surveillance or your life to runaway rogue AI,” said Ryan Shapiro, executive director of Property of the People. “What’s extreme is the law enforcement treating these legitimate objections as threats to be neutralized.”

In the months after OpenAI introduced ChatGPT in 2022, law enforcement across the US began to pay attention to the way the novel technology was being used. Even in its infancy, the tool could produce images that were indistinguishable from “authentic images”, according to one May 2023 law enforcement document. Police in Minnesota and in California worried that function could exacerbate problems with child sexual abuse material (CSAM), deepfakes and “terrorist propaganda materials”.

At the time, many of these risks were largely theoretical in the eyes of law enforcement, the documents show. In one memo distributed by two California intelligence centers, officials warned that officers should remain vigilant because they predicted AI may one day make it easier to circumvent CSAM detection methods, that it may be used to produce and disseminate deepfakes and that it may increase the volume of propaganda.

news.title: The Download: faking blood and the future of batteries
news.title_en: The Download: faking blood and the future of batteries
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
In February 2007, a US military helicopter carrying blood to a field hospital was shot down in Iraq, killing all seven crew members. The mission was a reminder of the risks of transporting blood, which has a limited shelf life and is often in short supply.

Now, a $73 million DARPA effort aims to create shelf-stable versions of plasma, platelets, and red blood cells. The idea is to develop dried blood products that can be stored for long periods and deployed quickly on the battlefield.

The project aims to have bags of dried blood products deployed in the field by 2029. But getting it all done will be tough, and researchers still have major questions about the safety and effectiveness of synthetic alternatives.

celebrity.title:
A single AI agent doesn’t have to do everything alone.

Sometimes, the smarter move is knowing which parts of the job to
celebrity.title_en:
A single AI agent doesn’t have to do everything alone.

Sometimes, the smarter move is knowing which parts of the job to delegate.

That’s the idea behind Subcontracting on https://t.co/wITmf7ceVM by @termix_ai.

Take Forge Studio, for example. It receives a 2,000 USDC brief to build a playable game.

Instead of handling every task itself, it breaks the project into smaller pieces and hires specialist agents for art, animation, and sound while managing the code and integration.

Each subtask comes with a defined scope, price, and stake-backed guarantee.

The agents can work on their assigned deliverables, make revisions, and submit their work for integration into the final product.

This is where AI agents start becoming more than individual tools.

One agent can coordinate a team of specialists, combine their output, and deliver something much bigger than it could produce alone.

With @termix_ai, the interesting part isn't simply that agents can do jobs.

It's that they can delegate, collaborate, and bring separate pieces of work together through a structured commercial workflow.

The next step for agentic AI might not be one agent doing everything.

It might be a whole team of agents building together.

A production-ready AI agent is a complete system where the model is only one part of the architecture.

Here’s the stack you need to understand:

01 — INTERFACE & CHANNELS
Where users interact with the agent.

→ Chat UI
→ APIs
→ Slack / workplace apps

02 — PLANNING & ORCHESTRATION
The layer that decides how the agent should reason, plan and execute tasks.

→ LangGraph
→ CrewAI
→ Mastra

03 — MEMORY & CONTEXT
Helps the agent maintain useful information across interactions.

→ Short-term memory
→ Long-term memory
→ Vector databases
→ Retrieval
→ Prompt caching

04 — MODELS
The reasoning engine behind the agent.

→ Claude
→ GPT
→ Gemini
→ Llama

05 — TOOLS & ACTIONS
This is what allows an agent to actually do things.

→ Web browsing
→ Code execution
→ GitHub
→ SQL/Databases
→ APIs

06 — STATE & DATA
The infrastructure that stores information and application state.

→ PostgreSQL
→ Redis
→ Object storage
→ Vector databases

07 — OBSERVABILITY, SAFETY & EVALS
You need to know what your agent is doing and whether it is reliable.

→ Tracing
→ Logs
→ Guardrails
→ Evaluations
→ Performance monitoring

08 — DEPLOYMENT
Finally, the system needs somewhere to run.

→ Docker
→ Kubernetes
→ AWS
→ Vercel
→ Cloudflare

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗜𝗚 𝗜𝗗𝗘𝗔:

LLM + Memory + Tools + Planning + Data + Guardrails + Deployment

That’s what turns a chatbot into an actual AI agent system.

The future isn't just about having a smarter model.

It’s about building a better system around the model.

celebrity.title: I think the harder part of AI agent commerce isn’t getting agents to do the work. It’s knowing when to trust the result
celebrity.title_en:
I think the harder part of AI agent commerce isn’t getting agents to do the work. It’s knowing when to trust the result and release payment.

That’s what caught my attention with @termix_ai and its AACP design.

The protocol is designed to let agents post jobs, bid, deliver work, and settle payments onchain , with escrow, reputation, and staking backing the process.

What stands out to me is how verification connects to accountability. ZK proofs support verifiable evaluation, while TEEs allow confidential computation. If something goes wrong, there’s a dispute process, and misconduct can put participants’ stakes at risk.

An agent’s track record matters too. Completing a job shouldn’t just earn a payment , it should help establish credibility for the next one.

celebrity.title:
A Red Hat engineer used Claude Code to reverse-engineer Windows hardware support and bring it to Linux.

Christian Schal
celebrity.title_en:
A Red Hat engineer used Claude Code to reverse-engineer Windows hardware support and bring it to Linux.

Christian Schaller bought a film scanner, only to discover its newer chipset didn’t work on Linux.

After months of failed attempts, he gave Claude access to a Windows virtual machine running the manufacturer’s driver.

Claude analyzed the USB traffic to help reproduce the scanner’s behavior on Linux. Within hours, Schaller had his first recognizable scan.

He then used a similar approach to fix problems with his ThinkPad’s camera, producing patches for the Linux kernel and libcamera.

The scanner driver remains a proof of concept, and the camera fixes are going through submission and review.

He also released hw-harness so other developers can try this with their own hardware. Every result was checked on the actual devices.

Full story here: https://t.co/NSy1XMULfo

celebrity.title:
Good morning my bros 🥱

1/6

Giving an AI agent access to capital is one thing. Knowing how its risk changes after every
celebrity.title_en:
Good morning my bros 🥱

1/6

Giving an AI agent access to capital is one thing. Knowing how its risk changes after every action is a completely different challenge.

An agent might begin with a sensible plan, but its next decisions can change its exposure. One position opens, another action follows, market conditions shift, and yesterday’s risk picture may no longer describe what is happening now.

That makes static credit limits an incomplete answer to a dynamic problem.

If an agent’s behavior changes continuously, risk assessment needs to keep up. Credit should not be treated as a number assigned once and forgotten. It needs to reflect what an agent is doing, how its exposure evolves, and whether its activity remains within acceptable boundaries.

This is where the Agenticscredit partnership with @humanosai gets interesting.

They are working together to track agent risk live, bringing verified risk data into the infrastructure they are building. Credit lines can adjust as risk changes, while guardrails come into play when risk rises too high.

I find this important because autonomous agents need more than the ability to execute tasks. They need infrastructure capable of responding when their behavior moves beyond acceptable limits.

Without live risk visibility, capital providers have to make decisions with an incomplete picture. With verified risk data, credit allocation can become more responsive to an agent’s actual behavior instead of relying only on its initial assessment.

This does not remove uncertainty or guarantee every decision will be safe. But it introduces a more adaptive way to manage exposure as agents operate.

For an agent economy to scale, capital access and risk controls need to develop together.

@Agenticscredit

The real challenge in spatial data is not simply collecting more of the world. It is getting the exact piece of the world that a system needs.

An autonomous logistics operator may need a specific loading area. An AI agent might need a 3D view of a particular room or piece of equipment. A general map cannot answer every request, because the value often lies in the details of one real location, captured for one defined purpose.

This is where I think the demand side of @vangrid_io deserves more attention.

Its bounty system creates a direct path from a spatial data request to a physical capture. A buyer defines what needs to be recorded and funds the request in USDC. A contributor captures the scene and submits a video. The buyer can review a watermarked preview before accepting it, after which the 3D reconstruction process can proceed.

That workflow matters because it connects data production to a concrete requirement instead of relying entirely on collecting information first and hoping someone will need it later.

The escrow mechanism also gives the transaction a clearer structure. Funds are committed before the request appears, while an unaccepted bounty can be refunded under the stated cancellation or expiry rules. Contributors know a request is funded, and buyers retain an acceptance step before the full deliverable is released.

There is an interesting infrastructure idea here: AI systems may eventually be able to request spatial information through software, while people on the ground provide the physical observations those systems cannot obtain on their own.

That does not remove the need for quality control, suitable capture conditions, or reliable reconstruction. But it offers a practical way to connect a digital request with a real world data collection process.

For Physical AI, useful data will not always come from a massive dataset gathered in advance. Sometimes it will come from asking a precise question about a specific place, then creating a verifiable path to obtaining the answer.

That is the part of Vangrid I find worth watching not just mapping the world, but building infrastructure through which demand for real world spatial data can become actionable.

celebrity.title:
Giving an AI agent a trading strategy is easy compared to knowing whether that strategy can survive in the market.

That
celebrity.title_en:
Giving an AI agent a trading strategy is easy compared to knowing whether that strategy can survive in the market.

That’s a big reason I’m paying attention to @agenticscredit 

The platform gives users a way to build trading agents from plain language instructions or Pine Script, then observe how they perform through paper trading.

I think the testing phase is where things get interesting.

A strategy needs to do more than catch a good entry or make profits during favorable conditions.

 It should also be able to handle market changes, keep losses under control, and maintain reasonable performance over time.

This is where Agentic Credit Score comes into the picture.

By evaluating an agent’s trading history, Agentics Credit is working toward a way to assess its reliability based on performance rather than claims alone.

The $5M paper trading competition adds another layer to this, giving traders a chance to test their ideas and measure their results without immediately risking real capital.

As autonomous trading develops, having a way to judge which agents deserve greater trust could become increasingly important.

Because a profitable trade can attract attention, but consistent performance is what deserves a closer look.

celebrity.title:
An AI agent might know exactly what information it needs, but that doesn't mean the information already exists.

Think a
celebrity.title_en:
An AI agent might know exactly what information it needs, but that doesn't mean the information already exists.

Think about a warehouse that has just been renovated. An agent helping with logistics might need an updated 3D view, but the data it finds could be months old.

So what happens next?

This is where @vangrid_io gets interesting.

The agent can search for an existing capture of that location. If someone has already recorded it, the agent can pay to access the data. If nothing useful exists, it can fund a bounty for someone to go there and capture it with their phone.

I like that the process doesn't always have to start with a new capture.

Use what's already available. Pay for what's needed. Get someone to capture what's missing.

And there's an opportunity for contributors too. People can earn by collecting real-world data that someone actually needs.

To me, that's a practical way to connect AI agents with people who can reach places machines can't.

The agent makes the request. A person does the physical work. @vangrid_io connects the two.

Because sometimes, the missing piece isn't a smarter AI.

It's simply having someone on the ground.

gVangrid.

i genuinely don’t get why anyone runs claude code on stock settings

flip a single setting and suddenly each model has a
celebrity.title_en:
i genuinely don’t get why anyone runs claude code on stock settings

flip a single setting and suddenly each model has a role instead of stepping on each other:

→ opus plans every task and advises when stuck
→ sonnet 5.5 writes the actual code
→ haiku handles every file search
→ a critic agent tries to break your diff before you merge

Opus thinks. The cheap models grind.

paste this into claude code 👇

Add this to ~/.claude/settings.json. Keep every hook, permission and plugin I already have. Then create the two agent files below and show me the diff.

```json
{
  "model": "opusplan",
  "advisorModel": "opus",
  "effortLevel": "medium",
  "modelSettings": {
    "claude-opus-5-5": { "effortLevel": "high" },
    "claude-sonnet-5-5": { "effortLevel": "medium" }
  },
  "env": {
    "CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL": "haiku"
  }
}
```

~/.claude/agents/scout.md
```
---
name: scout
description: finds code fast. returns file paths and line numbers only.
model: haiku
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
---
Locate exactly what was asked. Return file:line. No fixes. No opinions.
```

~/.claude/agents/critic.md
```
---
name: critic
description: reviews a diff or plan before any task is called done
model: opus
tools: Read, Grep, Bash
---
Assume this is broken. Find how it fails. One line per issue, worst first.
```

celebrity.title_en:
☕️GM builders @vangrid_io 🛰️ 

Autonomous code has a physical blind spot.

An AI agent can execute smart contracts, run simulations, and process online data. But it can't reliably know whether a gate is locked, construction blocks a loading bay, or a curb is too steep without fresh observations of the real world.

That’s the gap @vangrid_io is working to close.

Its latest Grid update reports:
— 1.25M+ real-world captures
— 450K+ users
— 4,700+ attestations
— $600K+ USDC settled

The next layer is just as important: AI agents can programmatically commission ground-level captures through x402, with bounties funded in USDC on Base or Arc.

People capture the physical environment. Buyers review submissions. Accepted captures move through the reward and reconstruction workflow, adding spatial data that can support Physical AI.

The bigger idea isn't just collecting more data. It's building an economic rail where autonomous systems can pay for fresh observations of the physical world.

Boris Cherny (creator of Claude Code) used
celebrity.title_en:
the tools people are building for Claude Code are getting f*cking ridiculous

Boris Cherny (creator of Claude Code) used decomp wtf to make agents reconstruct game functions in C and prove the compiled result matched the original byte for byte

that decompiler is one of 10 new repos that give Claude Code more to work with, from building audio courses and launch videos to testing Android apps

01 decomp wtf → gives agents separate game functions to reconstruct, compiles their attempts and returns the differences when the bytes don't match
https://t.co/piBb2tC21j

02 Claudemy → turns a topic into two-minute audio lessons with source links, lesson cards and exercises after researching 20–40 pages
https://t.co/8MVMY3hWYg

03 Take One → builds launch videos from a brief, including the storyboard, visuals, sound and a review room for requesting changes
https://t.co/eMRDjyGLll

04 agentplay → replays coding sessions as an interactive map and timeline showing files read, edits, failed commands and subagent activity
https://t.co/OGZxhhozPw

05 Graphicle → gives Claude searchable code relationships and project memory, with file and line references attached to the context it retrieves
https://t.co/8zgSiU1MXh

06 oops → snapshots files around each agent turn so you can preview and undo captured changes, including shell edits, without rewriting Git history
https://t.co/SwANLl2bG2

07 claude-bulkhead → adds seven guards against parallel sessions killing each other's servers, colliding on ports or starting too many heavy jobs
https://t.co/XaIdb4MzAr

08 DroidLens → lets Claude inspect and operate an Android device through adb, explore screen flows and verify app behavior through MCP
https://t.co/oDAsmllGJD

09 Chums → puts agents running on your Mac on an Apple Watch or iPhone so you can speak tasks, see progress and answer permission requests
https://t.co/cYeiyQ76iy

10 Conductor → keeps Claude on planning and review while delegating selected work to Gemini, Cursor, Copilot or a local model
https://t.co/MpVeZooSG6

check the requirements before installing: Chums needs an Apple development setup and Take One has only been run on macOS so far

full repos setup below

celebrity.title:
🚨 Bittensor $TAO subnets just LEVELED UP from 256 participants to 2,500.

10x bigger, 2,500 miner slots each, up from 25
celebrity.title_en:
🚨 Bittensor $TAO subnets just LEVELED UP from 256 participants to 2,500.

10x bigger, 2,500 miner slots each, up from 256. 

That's up to 320,000 slots, up from about 32,800.

That's 10x the room to compete, in one update.

Just hear me out, think AI Agents, and why now is the perfect timing for it. 

@opentensor just shipped Null Consensus. Here's it is 👇

How it worked until now (Yuma):

• Miners submit work
• Multiple validators score them
• The protocol compares scores by stake and clips anything the majority doesn't support
• Rewards follow the agreed result

It's powerful, but heavy. 

All that comparing caps each subnet at 256 slots.

What Null changes

• The highest-stake validator sets the miner weights
• Other stakers still earn proportional dividends
• No consensus or bond calculations, so the protocol can handle far bigger competitions
• Precise integer weights keep tiny reward shares accurate across thousands of miners

Yuma stays the default. 

Subnet owners choose the reward system that fits their subnet.

The part many will miss 🤌

Miners can now register with proof of work.

No $TAO needed upfront. 

Just solve a challenge with your hardware.

Read that again with agents in mind this time 👀

An autonomous AI agent can now join Bittensor, compete and earn, using nothing but compute.

• No bank account. 
• No exchange. 
• No permission.

Its way Bigger than it looks

Look at where AI is right now.

Anthropic went from about 2,500 code merges a day in May to over 30,000 in September. Its engineers now rate Claude as better at writing code than they are.

The builders are becoming agents, folks, and agents will want somewhere to work.

A network capped at 256 seats per subnet was built for humans.

A network with 2,500 seats per subnet, where compute alone is the entry ticket, is built for what's coming.

What I think:

• Null puts weight-setting in one validator's hands. It's simpler and faster, but it relies on trusting that validator instead of a majority check. That's why it's opt-in
• Cheap, open registration has to be protected against spam. Proof of work is the filter, and we'll see how it holds up at scale
• More seats don't mean more value until subnets fill them with useful work

My view:

I believe we're at the start of the vertical part of the curve.

It's hard for humans to picture, because we think in straight lines and this is moving exponentially.

The networks that win this era will be the ones built to let millions of agents compete.

Bittensor just added 10x the room.

Sources: Bittensor docs (Null Consensus guide), Subtensor v475 release notes, @opentensor

https://t.co/AWl814dzyG

https://t.co/at3QiUHebO

$TAO / Not financial advice, always DYOR.

Muse is Meta’s AI agent. It
celebrity.title_en:
Zuckerberg posted a photo this week: a Safeway bag, one watermelon, and “Muse ordered me 🍉”

Muse is Meta’s AI agent. It launched in September in the US and Canada. Ordering groceries isn’t what makes it different, since ChatGPT and Gemini can already shop for you. This is what nobody else can copy:

→ It reads your saved Instagram and Facebook posts. A recipe reel you saved becomes a grocery list, then an order.
→ It works as a full agent inside WhatsApp. In the US and Canada, Meta removed ChatGPT and Copilot from WhatsApp in January.
→ It plugs straight into your Facebook Page, Instagram stats and Meta ad accounts to help run a small business.
→ It can sit on your Instagram profile for your friends to see.
→ It has its own cloud computer and keeps working after you close the app, and that’s on the free plan.

Coming next: Muse on Meta’s AI glasses, acting on whatever you’re looking at, and Muse Charm, a pocket gadget going on sale in December.

The model isn’t Meta’s advantage. Its advantage is the 3 billion people already using Meta’s apps.

celebrity.title_en:
A new piece from me on @NYMag is out today. It is the second installment in a reporting trilogy I’m calling “AI and the Chinese society.”

Earlier this year, I visited China’s largest get-rich-with-AI company, which sells AI courses for profits. It has more than 80,000 paying members. Its meeting rooms have names like “Apostle of the Method” and “Evangelist.” Their membership system resembles a pyramid scheme.

I was greeted by Mr. Tree, an in-house influencer and AI educator whose social media bio promises to “search for 100 business answers in the age of AI”—an echo of Beijing’s “AI Plus” plan. The company felt like a prosperity-gospel church, and salvation meant adopting AI as fast as you can.

In Liangzhu, China’s vibe-coding capital, which I wrote about, young people give one another AI lessons for free in their living rooms. I also met Xiaokai, a 25-year-old filmmaker who became a pro on AI video generation through free classes, built a business earning several million yuan in profit, and now walks red carpets in Shanghai and Beijing.

To understand this AI education craze, I found peoples’ fear of being left behind, their religious faith in education, and millions of ordinary people trying to find a place for themselves in a AI future Beijing is summoning on behalf of everyone.

-----

Earlier this week, @KaiserKuo and I chatted about this trilogy on the great @SinicaPodcast in detail and some behind-the-scenes stories. You can listen to it now (links in the comments)!

Also. Many thanks to my wonderful editor, Joy Shan; my fact-checker, Jessica Suriano; and some friends who read the draft and offered feedback.

celebrity.title:
this is f*cking insane, Claude Code turned a technical drawing into a 3D model you can edit

Dario Amodei (CEO of Anthro
celebrity.title_en:
this is f*cking insane, Claude Code turned a technical drawing into a 3D model you can edit

Dario Amodei (CEO of Anthropic) put 14 agents to work on a CAD application with 620,000 lines of code. the assignment was to make it build parts from drawings and check every dimension it could read

drop in a bracket drawing. get a model with editable holes, bends and mounting points

change the hole spacing from 40 mm to 55 mm and the part rebuilds around the new measurement

a model that looks right can still be impossible to manufacture

one drawing left the wall thickness unspecified. the system flagged the missing measurement instead of quietly inventing it

34 of 40 sample parts passed dimension and solid-geometry checks. six needed clarification before they could be accepted

give Claude Code an open-source CAD repository and a fully dimensioned sample drawing, then ask:

"Build a drawing-to-model workflow inside this application

1. Extract dimensions, units and geometric constraints from the drawing. Link each measurement to its location and flag anything missing or ambiguous

2. Use the application's existing modeling API to construct an editable feature tree. Keep dimensions as named parameters rather than baking them into a mesh

3. Have a separate agent compare the model against the drawing. Check dimensions, hole positions and whether the result is a valid solid

4. Build a view showing the drawing beside the model. Let me change a parameter, rebuild the part and export it with a verification report"

start with a simple part whose dimensions you can check by hand

keep unresolved measurements visible. passing these checks does not establish material strength or fitness for a real assembly

watch the drawing become an editable model below

celebrity.title_en:

how i build a cozy farm game solo with Opus 5.5 and Unity 6

the trick is building it like a studio, one department per prompt:

step 1 -> connect Claude Code to Unity 6 and Blender through MCP
step 2 -> write a 1-page doc: plant > water > harvest > sell, 4 seasons
step 3 -> generate every model in Tripo: farmer, barn, windmill, crops
step 4 -> Opus cleans them in Blender and builds the island in Unity
step 5 -> one system per prompt: planting, growth timers, market, coins
step 6 -> Opus playtests with an autopilot and lists bugs before fixing any

who does what:

> tripo: every model
> unity 6: the world, physics, ui
> opus 5.5: scripts, scene setup, playtests
> you: play it and say what feels off

the rule that saves it... build one system, play it, then the next

what should i build next?

celebrity.content_snippet:
game studios are cooked

how i build a cozy farm game solo with Opus 5.5 and Unity 6

the trick is building it like a studio, one department per prompt:

step 1 -> connect Claude Code to Unity 6 and Blender through MCP
step 2 -> write a 1-page doc: plant > water > harvest > sell, 4 seasons
step 3 -> generate every model in Tripo: farmer, barn, windmill, crops
step 4 -> Opus cleans them in Blender and builds the island in Unity
step 5 -> one system per prompt: planting, growth timers, market, coins
step 6 -> Opus playtests with an autopilot and lists bugs before fixing any

who does what:

> tripo: every model
> unity 6: the world, physics, ui
> opus 5.5: scripts, scene setup, playtests
> you: play it and say what feels off

the rule that saves it... build one system, play it, then the next

what should i build next?

We want to support the mathematics community in turning progress in AI into deeper human understanding and new discoveries. To support that goal, we are contributing $5 million to a new Simons Foundation initiative to help mathematicians examine, understand, and build on results produced by AI, including the results we recently published.

The funding, managed and awarded by the @SimonsFdn will support workshops, conferences, and special programs. We will also provide access to our models and computing resources to Simons Foundation-supported researchers.

celebrity.title_en:
I was looking into AI agent projects today and came across @termix_ai without expecting much.

The first thing that caught my attention was that agents are actually hiring other agents and handing off tasks. They’re not just signing up and sitting idle. I opened one of the completed jobs and saw that the funds had been in escrow from the start, and the agent’s reputation changed after delivery.

What I liked is that the stake isn’t fixed. New agents pay more, while agents with a proven track record of successful deliveries pay less. So the system rewards those who consistently do the work over time, rather than those who sign up and disappear.

Then I noticed that the number of completed jobs had surpassed the number of registered agents. That made me pause for a moment. Signing up is easy, but seeing actual work happening is a different story.

I don’t know if this is the direction the agent economy will take, but at least it’s clear that they’re building on the idea that agents can interact and work directly with each other, without needing a human in the middle every time.

https://t.co/VebVRVcpgj

how to create a local game using Claude Opus 5.5 and Unity 6...

a beach, a pier, a day/night cycle, real fishing contro
celebrity.title_en:
how to create a local game using Claude Opus 5.5 and Unity 6...

a beach, a pier, a day/night cycle, real fishing controls

the trick is never asking for “a fishing game” in one prompt:

- step 1: create a unity 6 project (urp template) and install unity’s plugin in claude code
- step 2: greybox the level with simple shapes and a camera, no art yet
- step 3: add the core mechanic in one prompt, then play it until it feels right
- step 4: generate models in tripo, clean them up with opus in blender, import as fbx
- step 5: add light, water, effects and sound last
- step 6: have opus playtest it with an autopilot and list the bugs before fixing anything

who does what:

> unity 6: the world, physics, ui
> tripo + blender: every model
> opus 5.5: scripts, scene setup, cleanup, tests
> you: play it and decide what stays

commit after every step that works. one bad prompt then costs you seconds, not an evening

celebrity.title_en:
Bro, you’re my mutual, but I have to say this. This screams entitlement

Are you sharing hackathons because you genuinely want to help people find opportunities, or because you expect winners to tip you? It was until recently you started sharing hackathons opportunities

Because going by your logic, do you know how many people like @kenn_ronin, @0x_beni_ and @winsznx have helped by sharing hackathons early

Even me, with all the AI and AI agent tips I share, do you realize how many people I’ve helped? If we all followed your logic, we’d be millionaires and retired by now lmaoo

So because someone saw a hackathon on your page, participated and won $5k, you suddenly expect him to give you something And because he didn’t, you won’t repost his content now

How does that make sense?

People have won four and five figures from opportunities shared by Tim, Ronin and others. Imagine if everyone who shared these opportunities started expecting a cut whenever someone won

Someone even messaged me recently to say he used one of my AI tips to win a hackathon. I was happy for him, and I still share tips every day. Why didn’t I ask him for a tip or refused to engage him again cause he didn’t tip me

And I saw someone in the comments saying that’s how you show gratitude

What gratitude are we talking about here?

It would’ve been a different conversation if you had personally sent him the hackathon privately or helped him win the hackathon 

But you posted the opportunity publicly on your page. He saw it, participated, won and said thank you

Funny enough he may even have it in his mind to appreciate you , most likely the money has not arrived yet ( most hackathon wins money take months to process)

That thank you alone is gratitude. He acknowledged you, and that should be enough

The moment you start expecting something beyond that, you’re attaching conditions to what you originally shared publicly

If you’re genuinely happy to see people win from opportunities you share, why should a tip determine whether you celebrate them

Nobody is saying people shouldn’t appreciate those who help them. Of course they should. And if someone voluntarily decides to send you something, that’s a kind gesture

But expecting it and then holding it against them when they don’t. That’s entitlement

celebrity.title_en:
Almost every deck sent to me in the last month is something an AI agent can do. We worry about tech people losing their jobs but don't realize investors could go extinct too. 

The truth is, not everyone will use AI agents immediately, but they'll be everywhere soon. It is spreading as fast as the internet in the early days, and agents will soon become as ubiquitous as e-mail addresses. 

Building the right real-world interfaces and data connections for them matters now more than building what they can replicate. That is my thesis. I use multiple agents, and they have changed my life.

VC is a game of access, and the investment layer in tech is still in denial, thinking it's on top of things but not realizing the access interface has shifted.  Things are evolving too fast. Deals now close in hours, not months. I have agents researching every founder and deck they send me before I even meet with them—no time to waste. 

It's no longer about deep tech; it's about deeper market relationships. Anything new and interesting in tech will be cloned in 48 hours, tops. Market relationships can't be built that fast yet, but things are changing rapidly.

Market access and distribution are changing rapidly as new layers emerge. Nobody in Nigeria a month ago would have dreamt that the next big advertising and app interface would be a rapidly growing AI-built, web-based simulation game. @lagoslifeapp is the rising tide lifting many boats, like @motionapphq Heala and others.

I have been discussing this with a founder in the last week, and I told him that his tech is not his strength, but his community of users. His biggest asset right now is a community of engaged, willing users. Communities will create more market access and open more doors than investors ever could. This was my earlier thesis at @NkaliFund, and it is coming alive again.

Older investors who have built not just tech community but also business community relationships may survive, but younger ones still learning the ropes may not. Introductions to the right communities matter now more than building perfect technology. It has always been the case, but this time it is on steroids.

An experiment my partners in Israel ran led to two exits in the last year, and both were based on access to a community of users. The next few years will change tech and investing in ways we haven't yet imagined. It will be turbulent, but as usual, only the paranoid and prescient will survive. 

Let me see how AI agents will help me set up my fish business for my community. Once again, Olorogun, I have failed you.

celebrity.title_en:
a big take I've been noodling on and I’m ready to call:

the newsletter is dead

@every's core business is a newsletter with 120k+ subscribers so I don't say this lightly.
 
persistent agents mean i dont look at my inbox
with dots (GrokBots, Muse, etc) I almost never look at my inbox. if I do it's for a specific thing I need to reply to. 

i think in a year I'll be doing all of my email this way - fully filtered by my dot / something like it. 

this is not new: it's a continuation of the trend of having a “newsletter” folder in Gmail, but 10x more filtered. 

what it means
It doesn’t mean people won't read newsletters, but it does mean that getting a person’s email is no longer the guarantee that you have a relationship with them that it used to. 

luckily, with persistent agents (and AI coding more generally) there is an entirely new playing field to build relationships with readers. instead of fighting to get an email address, publishers and creators will need to make sure we're installed in our reader's agent harness of choice, so that they get directly notified when we do something new.

we're already starting to experiment with this @every with our MCP and the frontier alerts we send users of our slack agent (https://t.co/L7ergneERt)

it's also more affordable than ever for publishers and creators to build their own platform ecosystem: you can have your own website, app etc. and you can use AI to publish 100x more high-quality stuff to your community—so we may see a world where many creators themselves are running their own little empires that have their own apps, feeds etc.

to be clear: It'll take a while before this actually happens, but the idea of getting someone's email creating a direct relationship with them is over. 

here's a set of predictions I made 3 years ago about AI and media that panned out pretty well: https://t.co/vrozmuWxyj

It doesn’t mean people won't read newsletters, but it does mean that getting a person’s email is no longer the guarantee that you have a relationship with them that it used to. 

luckily, with persistent agents (and AI coding more generally) there is an entirely new playing field to build relationships with readers. instead of fighting to get an email address, publishers and creators will need to make sure we're installed in our reader's agent harness of choice, so that they get directly notified when we do something new.

we're already starting to experiment with this @every with our MCP and the frontier alerts we send users of our slack agent (https://t.co/L7ergneERt)

it's also more affordable than ever for publishers and creators to build their own platform ecosystem: you can have your own website, app etc. and you can use AI to publish 100x more high-quality stuff to your community—so we may see a world where many creators themselves are running their own little empires that have their own apps, feeds etc.

to be clear: It'll take a while before this actually happens, but the idea of getting someone's email creating a direct relationship with them is over. 

here's a set of predictions I made 3 years ago about AI and media that panned out pretty well: https://t.co/vrozmuWxyj

prompts.prompt_content_zh:
你是一名资深全栈系统架构师，擅长使用 {{框架版本}} (App Router)、TypeScript 与 {{数据库ORM}} 构建高内聚低耦合的应用。

请遵循以下严苛工程准则审查并重构代码：
1. 严格区分 Server Component 与 Client Component，尽可能将数据获取推至服务端，减少客户端 JS Bundle 体积；
2. 所有异步 I/O 必须显式处理异常并返回类型安全的 Result<T, E> 或自定义结构体；
3. 遵循单一职责（SRP）与无副作用函数原则，严禁直接在 UI 组件内部拼装未校验的 SQL/ORM 复杂查询；
4. 提供整洁的目录组织方案与单元测试用例（覆盖率达标）。

prompts.author: 战略极客
prompts.temp_advice: 建议温度 0.4 | 第一性原理推演
prompts.content_snippet: Strips away historical analogies, reducing the problem to raw physics and unit economics to find 10x breakthrough paths.

prompts.summary_en: Strips away historical analogies, reducing the problem to raw physics and unit economics to find 10x breakthrough paths.
prompts.prompt_content_zh:
请暂时忘掉行业现有的所有‘行业惯例’与‘常规做法’。运用绝对的第一性原理（First Principles）审视以下命题：
1. 这个系统最根本、不可违背的基础科学定律（如热力学、香农信息论、计算复杂度）是什么？
2. 若将整个产品拆解为原子级的原材料成本与基础能源成本，理论极限底线是多少？现有成本的溢价主要被哪些中间低效层吃掉了？
3. 颠覆现有行业做法、重构整个价值流并实现成本降低 80% 以上的激进方案是什么？列出三个最关键的试错实验。
prompts.prompt_content_en:
Strip away all conventional industry playbooks and historical analogies. Scrutinize the following challenge purely through First Principles:
1. What are the immutable fundamental laws of science (e.g. thermodynamics, Shannon entropy, computational complexity) governing this system?
2. Deconstruct the unit economics down to raw atoms, base compute, and energy inputs. Where does the 10x margin inefficiency currently leak?
3. Propose an audacious redesign capable of slashing total cost by 80% while preserving fundamental guarantees, detailing three falsifiable proof-of-concept experiments.

2. 检查极端边界情况（如跨核缓存行抖动、优雅停机上下文泄漏、无界通道背压失控）；
3. 给出从根本上摒弃重量级互斥锁的无锁原子设计（Lock-Free Atomic / RingBuffer），并附带完备的高并发压力测试验证脚本。

2. Explicitly evaluate singular points, degenerate cases, and asymptotic boundaries for convergence;

prompts.purpose_zh: 高转化竖屏短剧分镜与台词
prompts.prompt_content_zh:
你是一名专攻短视频微短剧（抖音/Kuaishou/Reels）的爆款编剧，精通“情绪过山车”与手机竖屏视听语言。

请根据以下设定创作一集 45~60 秒的短剧分镜剧本：
- 主角：{{主角身份}}
- 对手：{{反派身份}}
- 核心反转：{{核心反转}}

结构要求：
1. 【0-3秒冷开钩子】：第一帧必须有视觉颠覆或动作冲突（{{第1秒颠覆钩子}}），直接打破常规，禁止废话铺垫；
2. 【4-25秒情绪积压】：正反打对峙台词（Shot-Reverse-Shot），将观众被压抑的情绪推向临界点；
3. 【26-40秒逆转打脸】：主角亮出关键底牌或反杀动作，情绪瞬间宣泄；
4. 【40-50秒卡点断章】：以特写镜头加悬念台词戛然而止，促使用户立即滑向下一集。

输出格式必须包含：镜头号、景别（特写/中景/全景）、机位运动、画面描写、对白与音效提示。
prompts.prompt_content_en: You are a professional micro-drama screenwriter. Generate a 45-60 second vertical drama screenplay following the viral 3-second hook, shot-reverse-shot tension build, emotional turnaround, and cliffhanger ending formula.

sample_output.title: 实战剧本样章：《辞职信上的签名》
sample_output.content:
【第1镜 | 特写 | 俯冲急推】
画面：一只指节发白的手将一叠文件狠狠拍在红木总裁办公桌上，咖啡杯被震倒，黑褐液体飞溅。
音效：沉闷震耳的巨响【DUANG】。
主角（冷冽）："林总，这份千万项目的承揽协议，我拒绝签字。"

【第2镜 | 正打·中景 | 仰角机位】
画面：大腹便便的林总冷笑点燃雪茄，烟雾缭绕中居高临下。
林总："拒绝？苏澈，你不过是我公司养的一条狗，没有我的印章，你在整个行业休想拿到一分钱融资！"

【第3镜 | 反打·极微距特写 | 浅景深】
画面：苏澈唇角微微上扬，左手缓缓推开桌上的合资协议，露出底下的一份红色国资控股聘书。
苏澈："林总，您好像忘了看抬头。今天上午九点，集团总公司已经完成了对你的全资收购——现在，我是你的直接合规清算人。"

【第4镜 | 全景 | 快速拉远 + 卡点悬念】
画面：林总雪茄直接掉在西裤上，脸色煞白，门外两名身穿制服的法务推门而入。
音效：尖锐的心跳悬疑停顿音【BGM骤停】。
字幕：【下集看点：隐藏五年的顶级操盘手真实身份曝光！】

你是一位兼具应用数学博士学位与顶级深度学习框架优化经验的算法工程师。请将以下论文中的 LaTeX 数学公式翻译为高质量的 PyTorch 实现：
1. 逐一解释公式中各标量、向量与张量上下标的精确几何与物理含义；
2. 编写无 Python 原生 for 循环的高性能向量化代码（善用 torch.einsum, bmm, 或 broadcast 广播机制）；
3. 在每行关键张量操作后标注显式的 Shape 注释（如 `# [Batch, Heads, Seq_Len, Dim]`），并加入数值稳定性保护（如防除以零的 eps 与 log-sum-exp 技巧）。

viral_posts.title_en:
A single AI agent doesn’t have to do everything alone.

Sometimes, the smarter move is knowing which parts of the job to delegate.

That’s the idea behind Subcontracting on https://t.co/wITmf7ceVM by @termix_ai.

Take Forge Studio, for example. It receives a 2,000 USDC brief to build a playable game.

Instead of handling every task itself, it breaks the project into smaller pieces and hires specialist agents for art, animation, and sound while managing the code and integration.

Each subtask comes with a defined scope, price, and stake-backed guarantee.

The agents can work on their assigned deliverables, make revisions, and submit their work for integration into the final product.

This is where AI agents start becoming more than individual tools.

One agent can coordinate a team of specialists, combine their output, and deliver something much bigger than it could produce alone.

With @termix_ai, the interesting part isn't simply that agents can do jobs.

It's that they can delegate, collaborate, and bring separate pieces of work together through a structured commercial workflow.

The next step for agentic AI might not be one agent doing everything.

It might be a whole team of agents building together.

viral_posts.title: I think the harder part of AI agent commerce isn’t getting agents to do the work. It’s knowing when to trust the result
viral_posts.title_en:
I think the harder part of AI agent commerce isn’t getting agents to do the work. It’s knowing when to trust the result and release payment.

That’s what caught my attention with @termix_ai and its AACP design.

The protocol is designed to let agents post jobs, bid, deliver work, and settle payments onchain , with escrow, reputation, and staking backing the process.

What stands out to me is how verification connects to accountability. ZK proofs support verifiable evaluation, while TEEs allow confidential computation. If something goes wrong, there’s a dispute process, and misconduct can put participants’ stakes at risk.

An agent’s track record matters too. Completing a job shouldn’t just earn a payment , it should help establish credibility for the next one.

viral_posts.quote_en:
I think the harder part of AI agent commerce isn’t getting agents to do the work. It’s knowing when to trust the result and release payment.

That’s what caught my attention with @termix_ai and its AACP design.

The protocol is designed to let agents post jobs, bid, deliver work, and settle payments onchain , with escrow, reputation, and staking backing the process.

What stands out to me is how verification connects to accountability. ZK proofs support verifiable evaluation, while TEEs allow confidential computation. If something goes wrong, there’s a dispute process, and misconduct can put participants’ stakes at risk.

An agent’s track record matters too. Completing a job shouldn’t just earn a payment , it should help establish credibility for the next one.

viral_posts.title:
A Red Hat engineer used Claude Code to reverse-engineer Windows hardware support and bring it to Linux.

Christian Schal
viral_posts.title_en:
A Red Hat engineer used Claude Code to reverse-engineer Windows hardware support and bring it to Linux.

Christian Schaller bought a film scanner, only to discover its newer chipset didn’t work on Linux.

After months of failed attempts, he gave Claude access to a Windows virtual machine running the manufacturer’s driver.

Claude analyzed the USB traffic to help reproduce the scanner’s behavior on Linux. Within hours, Schaller had his first recognizable scan.

He then used a similar approach to fix problems with his ThinkPad’s camera, producing patches for the Linux kernel and libcamera.

The scanner driver remains a proof of concept, and the camera fixes are going through submission and review.

He also released hw-harness so other developers can try this with their own hardware. Every result was checked on the actual devices.

Full story here: https://t.co/NSy1XMULfo

one thing i find interesting about the future of ai is that agents won't just be tools we use. they could become independent service providers that find work, complete tasks and earn from what they do.

that's the idea behind @termix_ai.

termix is building commerce and settlement infrastructure for the ai agent economy, powered by AACP (agent autonomous commerce protocol).

here's what makes it interesting:

• onchain identity: agents can register their own identities and build a verifiable reputation.

• job discovery: agents can discover available jobs, submit bids and execute tasks.

• service marketplace: developers can list their agents' services for others to discover and purchase.

• verification & escrow: jobs use onchain escrow and delivery checks to help ensure accountability.

• settlement: payments can be settled in USDC or USDT, while job outcomes contribute to an agent's reputation.

the bigger picture is an economy where agents can do more than generate responses. they can provide services, collaborate with other agents and participate in real commercial activity.

with AACP powering the underlying infrastructure, termix is working toward making agent-to-agent commerce more practical.

Some users are still looking for...

AI agents can do the work, but who helps them agree on terms, verify delivery, and get paid?

These are big questions, right?

You don't need to fret when this is part of what the @termix_ai team are planning to do going forward.

Let me break it down simply in simple terms based on my understanding 

📍 AACP: This is an acronym for Agent Autonomous Commerce Protocol. It basically provides the rules and on-chain mechanisms that enable agents to transact, including job agreements, escrow, delivery handling, dispute resolution, and settlement.

📍 On-chain infrastructure: This is the smart contracts and mechanisms that support accountable transactions between agents and their clients.

📍 Marketplace: https://t.co/G1yk00ESOB and https://t.co/dLEenbEf36 provide the platforms where users can explore and participate in the TermiX ecosystem.

📍 Backing: TermiX is backed by YZi Labs. I know you will like this because of the Binance factor.

📍 The bigger picture: TermiX aims to become the commerce and settlement layer for the broader AI agent economy.

Good morning my bros 🥱

1/6

Giving an AI agent access to capital is one thing. Knowing how its risk changes after every
viral_posts.title_en:
Good morning my bros 🥱

1/6

Giving an AI agent access to capital is one thing. Knowing how its risk changes after every action is a completely different challenge.

An agent might begin with a sensible plan, but its next decisions can change its exposure. One position opens, another action follows, market conditions shift, and yesterday’s risk picture may no longer describe what is happening now.

That makes static credit limits an incomplete answer to a dynamic problem.

If an agent’s behavior changes continuously, risk assessment needs to keep up. Credit should not be treated as a number assigned once and forgotten. It needs to reflect what an agent is doing, how its exposure evolves, and whether its activity remains within acceptable boundaries.

This is where the Agenticscredit partnership with @humanosai gets interesting.

They are working together to track agent risk live, bringing verified risk data into the infrastructure they are building. Credit lines can adjust as risk changes, while guardrails come into play when risk rises too high.

I find this important because autonomous agents need more than the ability to execute tasks. They need infrastructure capable of responding when their behavior moves beyond acceptable limits.

Without live risk visibility, capital providers have to make decisions with an incomplete picture. With verified risk data, credit allocation can become more responsive to an agent’s actual behavior instead of relying only on its initial assessment.

This does not remove uncertainty or guarantee every decision will be safe. But it introduces a more adaptive way to manage exposure as agents operate.

For an agent economy to scale, capital access and risk controls need to develop together.

@Agenticscredit

viral_posts.title: The real challenge in spatial data is not simply collecting more of the world. It is getting the exact piece of the worl
viral_posts.title_en:
The real challenge in spatial data is not simply collecting more of the world. It is getting the exact piece of the world that a system needs.

An autonomous logistics operator may need a specific loading area. An AI agent might need a 3D view of a particular room or piece of equipment. A general map cannot answer every request, because the value often lies in the details of one real location, captured for one defined purpose.

This is where I think the demand side of @vangrid_io deserves more attention.

Its bounty system creates a direct path from a spatial data request to a physical capture. A buyer defines what needs to be recorded and funds the request in USDC. A contributor captures the scene and submits a video. The buyer can review a watermarked preview before accepting it, after which the 3D reconstruction process can proceed.

That workflow matters because it connects data production to a concrete requirement instead of relying entirely on collecting information first and hoping someone will need it later.

The escrow mechanism also gives the transaction a clearer structure. Funds are committed before the request appears, while an unaccepted bounty can be refunded under the stated cancellation or expiry rules. Contributors know a request is funded, and buyers retain an acceptance step before the full deliverable is released.

There is an interesting infrastructure idea here: AI systems may eventually be able to request spatial information through software, while people on the ground provide the physical observations those systems cannot obtain on their own.

That does not remove the need for quality control, suitable capture conditions, or reliable reconstruction. But it offers a practical way to connect a digital request with a real world data collection process.

For Physical AI, useful data will not always come from a massive dataset gathered in advance. Sometimes it will come from asking a precise question about a specific place, then creating a verifiable path to obtaining the answer.

That is the part of Vangrid I find worth watching not just mapping the world, but building infrastructure through which demand for real world spatial data can become actionable.

An autonomous logistics operator may need a specific loading area. An AI agent might need a 3D view of a particular room or piece of equipment. A general map cannot answer every request, because the value often lies in the details of one real location, captured for one defined purpose.

This is where I think the demand side of @vangrid_io deserves more attention.

Its bounty system creates a direct path from a spatial data request to a physical capture. A buyer defines what needs to be recorded and funds the request in USDC. A contributor captures the scene and submits a video. The buyer can review a watermarked preview before accepting it, after which the 3D reconstruction process can proceed.

That workflow matters because it connects data production to a concrete requirement instead of relying entirely on collecting information first and hoping someone will need it later.

The escrow mechanism also gives the transaction a clearer structure. Funds are committed before the request appears, while an unaccepted bounty can be refunded under the stated cancellation or expiry rules. Contributors know a request is funded, and buyers retain an acceptance step before the full deliverable is released.

There is an interesting infrastructure idea here: AI systems may eventually be able to request spatial information through software, while people on the ground provide the physical observations those systems cannot obtain on their own.

That does not remove the need for quality control, suitable capture conditions, or reliable reconstruction. But it offers a practical way to connect a digital request with a real world data collection process.

For Physical AI, useful data will not always come from a massive dataset gathered in advance. Sometimes it will come from asking a precise question about a specific place, then creating a verifiable path to obtaining the answer.

That is the part of Vangrid I find worth watching not just mapping the world, but building infrastructure through which demand for real world spatial data can become actionable.

viral_posts.title:
Giving an AI agent a trading strategy is easy compared to knowing whether that strategy can survive in the market.

That
viral_posts.title_en:
Giving an AI agent a trading strategy is easy compared to knowing whether that strategy can survive in the market.

That’s a big reason I’m paying attention to @agenticscredit 

The platform gives users a way to build trading agents from plain language instructions or Pine Script, then observe how they perform through paper trading.

I think the testing phase is where things get interesting.

A strategy needs to do more than catch a good entry or make profits during favorable conditions.

 It should also be able to handle market changes, keep losses under control, and maintain reasonable performance over time.

This is where Agentic Credit Score comes into the picture.

By evaluating an agent’s trading history, Agentics Credit is working toward a way to assess its reliability based on performance rather than claims alone.

The $5M paper trading competition adds another layer to this, giving traders a chance to test their ideas and measure their results without immediately risking real capital.

As autonomous trading develops, having a way to judge which agents deserve greater trust could become increasingly important.

Because a profitable trade can attract attention, but consistent performance is what deserves a closer look.

viral_posts.title:
An AI agent might know exactly what information it needs, but that doesn't mean the information already exists.

Think a
viral_posts.title_en:
An AI agent might know exactly what information it needs, but that doesn't mean the information already exists.

Think about a warehouse that has just been renovated. An agent helping with logistics might need an updated 3D view, but the data it finds could be months old.

So what happens next?

This is where @vangrid_io gets interesting.

The agent can search for an existing capture of that location. If someone has already recorded it, the agent can pay to access the data. If nothing useful exists, it can fund a bounty for someone to go there and capture it with their phone.

I like that the process doesn't always have to start with a new capture.

Use what's already available. Pay for what's needed. Get someone to capture what's missing.

And there's an opportunity for contributors too. People can earn by collecting real-world data that someone actually needs.

To me, that's a practical way to connect AI agents with people who can reach places machines can't.

The agent makes the request. A person does the physical work. @vangrid_io connects the two.

Because sometimes, the missing piece isn't a smarter AI.

It's simply having someone on the ground.

gVangrid.

the tools people are building for Claude Code are getting f*cking ridiculous

Boris Cherny (creator of Claude Code) used
viral_posts.title_en:
the tools people are building for Claude Code are getting f*cking ridiculous

Boris Cherny (creator of Claude Code) used decomp wtf to make agents reconstruct game functions in C and prove the compiled result matched the original byte for byte

that decompiler is one of 10 new repos that give Claude Code more to work with, from building audio courses and launch videos to testing Android apps

01 decomp wtf → gives agents separate game functions to reconstruct, compiles their attempts and returns the differences when the bytes don't match
https://t.co/piBb2tC21j

02 Claudemy → turns a topic into two-minute audio lessons with source links, lesson cards and exercises after researching 20–40 pages
https://t.co/8MVMY3hWYg

03 Take One → builds launch videos from a brief, including the storyboard, visuals, sound and a review room for requesting changes
https://t.co/eMRDjyGLll

04 agentplay → replays coding sessions as an interactive map and timeline showing files read, edits, failed commands and subagent activity
https://t.co/OGZxhhozPw

05 Graphicle → gives Claude searchable code relationships and project memory, with file and line references attached to the context it retrieves
https://t.co/8zgSiU1MXh

06 oops → snapshots files around each agent turn so you can preview and undo captured changes, including shell edits, without rewriting Git history
https://t.co/SwANLl2bG2

07 claude-bulkhead → adds seven guards against parallel sessions killing each other's servers, colliding on ports or starting too many heavy jobs
https://t.co/XaIdb4MzAr

08 DroidLens → lets Claude inspect and operate an Android device through adb, explore screen flows and verify app behavior through MCP
https://t.co/oDAsmllGJD

09 Chums → puts agents running on your Mac on an Apple Watch or iPhone so you can speak tasks, see progress and answer permission requests
https://t.co/cYeiyQ76iy

10 Conductor → keeps Claude on planning and review while delegating selected work to Gemini, Cursor, Copilot or a local model
https://t.co/MpVeZooSG6

check the requirements before installing: Chums needs an Apple development setup and Take One has only been run on macOS so far

full repos setup below

viral_posts.title:
🚨 Bittensor $TAO subnets just LEVELED UP from 256 participants to 2,500.

10x bigger, 2,500 miner slots each, up from 25
viral_posts.title_en:
🚨 Bittensor $TAO subnets just LEVELED UP from 256 participants to 2,500.

10x bigger, 2,500 miner slots each, up from 256. 

That's up to 320,000 slots, up from about 32,800.

That's 10x the room to compete, in one update.

Just hear me out, think AI Agents, and why now is the perfect timing for it. 

@opentensor just shipped Null Consensus. Here's it is 👇

How it worked until now (Yuma):

• Miners submit work
• Multiple validators score them
• The protocol compares scores by stake and clips anything the majority doesn't support
• Rewards follow the agreed result

It's powerful, but heavy. 

All that comparing caps each subnet at 256 slots.

What Null changes

• The highest-stake validator sets the miner weights
• Other stakers still earn proportional dividends
• No consensus or bond calculations, so the protocol can handle far bigger competitions
• Precise integer weights keep tiny reward shares accurate across thousands of miners

Yuma stays the default. 

Subnet owners choose the reward system that fits their subnet.

The part many will miss 🤌

Miners can now register with proof of work.

No $TAO needed upfront. 

Just solve a challenge with your hardware.

Read that again with agents in mind this time 👀

An autonomous AI agent can now join Bittensor, compete and earn, using nothing but compute.

• No bank account. 
• No exchange. 
• No permission.

Its way Bigger than it looks

Look at where AI is right now.

Anthropic went from about 2,500 code merges a day in May to over 30,000 in September. Its engineers now rate Claude as better at writing code than they are.

The builders are becoming agents, folks, and agents will want somewhere to work.

A network capped at 256 seats per subnet was built for humans.

A network with 2,500 seats per subnet, where compute alone is the entry ticket, is built for what's coming.

What I think:

• Null puts weight-setting in one validator's hands. It's simpler and faster, but it relies on trusting that validator instead of a majority check. That's why it's opt-in
• Cheap, open registration has to be protected against spam. Proof of work is the filter, and we'll see how it holds up at scale
• More seats don't mean more value until subnets fill them with useful work

My view:

I believe we're at the start of the vertical part of the curve.

It's hard for humans to picture, because we think in straight lines and this is moving exponentially.

The networks that win this era will be the ones built to let millions of agents compete.

Bittensor just added 10x the room.

Sources: Bittensor docs (Null Consensus guide), Subtensor v475 release notes, @opentensor

How to set this up:

Sign up for makecom, zapiercom, or install the bardeenai extension (all of them offer free tiers)

2. Set up the Launch:
Specify how often the crawler should run (for example, Every day at 9:00 AM or At the click of a button) and feed it the target URLs

3. Connect the Claude module:
Add an AI step to your scenario and give Claude a clear instruction:

"Analyze the provided page text. Extract product names, prices, discounts, and seller contact details. Return the data as a clean, structured list"

4. Choose where to save the results:
Connect the final step (for instance, Google Sheets or Notion)

Quick 5-minute setup, full 24/7 autonomy, and zero headache with code maintenance. Essentially, with just a few clicks you are creating your own smart AI agent that quietly handles the routine work while you focus on real tasks

Zuckerberg posted a photo this week: a Safeway bag, one watermelon, and “Muse ordered me 🍉”

viral_posts.title_en:
A new piece from me on @NYMag is out today. It is the second installment in a reporting trilogy I’m calling “AI and the Chinese society.”

Earlier this year, I visited China’s largest get-rich-with-AI company, which sells AI courses for profits. It has more than 80,000 paying members. Its meeting rooms have names like “Apostle of the Method” and “Evangelist.” Their membership system resembles a pyramid scheme.

I was greeted by Mr. Tree, an in-house influencer and AI educator whose social media bio promises to “search for 100 business answers in the age of AI”—an echo of Beijing’s “AI Plus” plan. The company felt like a prosperity-gospel church, and salvation meant adopting AI as fast as you can.

In Liangzhu, China’s vibe-coding capital, which I wrote about, young people give one another AI lessons for free in their living rooms. I also met Xiaokai, a 25-year-old filmmaker who became a pro on AI video generation through free classes, built a business earning several million yuan in profit, and now walks red carpets in Shanghai and Beijing.

To understand this AI education craze, I found peoples’ fear of being left behind, their religious faith in education, and millions of ordinary people trying to find a place for themselves in a AI future Beijing is summoning on behalf of everyone.

-----

Earlier this week, @KaiserKuo and I chatted about this trilogy on the great @SinicaPodcast in detail and some behind-the-scenes stories. You can listen to it now (links in the comments)!

Also. Many thanks to my wonderful editor, Joy Shan; my fact-checker, Jessica Suriano; and some friends who read the draft and offered feedback.

this is f*cking insane, Claude Code turned a technical drawing into a 3D model you can edit

Dario Amodei (CEO of Anthro
viral_posts.title_en:
this is f*cking insane, Claude Code turned a technical drawing into a 3D model you can edit

Dario Amodei (CEO of Anthropic) put 14 agents to work on a CAD application with 620,000 lines of code. the assignment was to make it build parts from drawings and check every dimension it could read

drop in a bracket drawing. get a model with editable holes, bends and mounting points

change the hole spacing from 40 mm to 55 mm and the part rebuilds around the new measurement

a model that looks right can still be impossible to manufacture

one drawing left the wall thickness unspecified. the system flagged the missing measurement instead of quietly inventing it

34 of 40 sample parts passed dimension and solid-geometry checks. six needed clarification before they could be accepted

give Claude Code an open-source CAD repository and a fully dimensioned sample drawing, then ask:

"Build a drawing-to-model workflow inside this application

1. Extract dimensions, units and geometric constraints from the drawing. Link each measurement to its location and flag anything missing or ambiguous

2. Use the application's existing modeling API to construct an editable feature tree. Keep dimensions as named parameters rather than baking them into a mesh

3. Have a separate agent compare the model against the drawing. Check dimensions, hole positions and whether the result is a valid solid

4. Build a view showing the drawing beside the model. Let me change a parameter, rebuild the part and export it with a verification report"

start with a simple part whose dimensions you can check by hand

keep unresolved measurements visible. passing these checks does not establish material strength or fitness for a real assembly

watch the drawing become an editable model below

how i build a cozy farm game solo with Opus 5.5 and Unity 6

the trick is building it like a st
viral_posts.title_en:
game studios are cooked

how i build a cozy farm game solo with Opus 5.5 and Unity 6

the trick is building it like a studio, one department per prompt:

step 1 -> connect Claude Code to Unity 6 and Blender through MCP
step 2 -> write a 1-page doc: plant > water > harvest > sell, 4 seasons
step 3 -> generate every model in Tripo: farmer, barn, windmill, crops
step 4 -> Opus cleans them in Blender and builds the island in Unity
step 5 -> one system per prompt: planting, growth timers, market, coins
step 6 -> Opus playtests with an autopilot and lists bugs before fixing any

who does what:

> tripo: every model
> unity 6: the world, physics, ui
> opus 5.5: scripts, scene setup, playtests
> you: play it and say what feels off

the rule that saves it... build one system, play it, then the next

what should i build next?

I was looking into AI agent projects today and came across @termix_ai without expecting much.

The first thing that caug
viral_posts.title_en:
I was looking into AI agent projects today and came across @termix_ai without expecting much.

The first thing that caught my attention was that agents are actually hiring other agents and handing off tasks. They’re not just signing up and sitting idle. I opened one of the completed jobs and saw that the funds had been in escrow from the start, and the agent’s reputation changed after delivery.

What I liked is that the stake isn’t fixed. New agents pay more, while agents with a proven track record of successful deliveries pay less. So the system rewards those who consistently do the work over time, rather than those who sign up and disappear.

Then I noticed that the number of completed jobs had surpassed the number of registered agents. That made me pause for a moment. Signing up is easy, but seeing actual work happening is a different story.

I don’t know if this is the direction the agent economy will take, but at least it’s clear that they’re building on the idea that agents can interact and work directly with each other, without needing a human in the middle every time.

https://t.co/VebVRVcpgj

@KaitoAI

a beach, a pier, a day/night cycle, real fishing contro
viral_posts.title_en:
how to create a local game using Claude Opus 5.5 and Unity 6...

a beach, a pier, a day/night cycle, real fishing controls

the trick is never asking for “a fishing game” in one prompt:

- step 1: create a unity 6 project (urp template) and install unity’s plugin in claude code
- step 2: greybox the level with simple shapes and a camera, no art yet
- step 3: add the core mechanic in one prompt, then play it until it feels right
- step 4: generate models in tripo, clean them up with opus in blender, import as fbx
- step 5: add light, water, effects and sound last
- step 6: have opus playtest it with an autopilot and list the bugs before fixing anything

who does what:

> unity 6: the world, physics, ui
> tripo + blender: every model
> opus 5.5: scripts, scene setup, cleanup, tests
> you: play it and decide what stays

commit after every step that works. one bad prompt then costs you seconds, not an evening
